I have to give my two cents on this game.

Disclaimer: I'm not very good at strategy games so this isn't going to reflect gameplay.

There are a number of intuitive issues with the game which makes it very difficult to navigate:

1) Even when not being shot at, when ordered your units will just decide to do nothing, absolutely nothing. They'll just stand there and I have to click multiple times to get them to do something. This makes ordering large number of units fustrating.

2) Ordering a group of units is fustrating as hell. They don't space out and just move in a conga line; there's no option to space them out as a group, leaving my tanks to get picked off one by one by the enemy. This makes frontal assaults difficult as hell.

3) People like this game for the level of micromanagement but most of this is difficult to find.

4) The Pathfinding is just bad, infantry and tanks just get stuck in specific places and I have to manually maneuver them to get where they need to go.

5) The micromanaging aspect is fustration: if I order a mortar team to attack somewhere, automatically they should just pick up and go until they reach the enemy. Instead, I need to order them to pick up their equipment and move out. 

For people who like autistic levels of details to do with military stuff, this is great. However, it's really unintuitive and expects you to do twice the work for very basic things.

222929426.review:
The best WW2 RTS out there. 

Pros: I can go on and on but I'll try to keep it short, and in no particular order.
1.) Extremely immersive, very realistic, and runs very well even if you don't have a beast PC. It has a pretty steep learning curve because of the sheer amount of game mechanics that the game has, and this is what makes the game so fun imo. I'm still learning new things almost 300 hours into it.
2.) You can take personal control of individual vehicles in either first, or third-person perspectives. You can also take control of individual soldiers in a third-person perspective. This makes the ground vehicle combat feel damn near as good as Warthunder(not to mention the similar armor penetration mechanics), and adds another layer of fun + immersion to the infantry combat. 
3.) If you're a history buff like me, the attention to detail for the time period really stands out. Vehicles for all nations look, sound, and feel authentic. The soldiers for every nation also look and sound authentic for the time period, along with historically accurate weaponry + equipment. 
4.) The diversity of vehicles and infantry units is actually insane. There has to be hundreds of different vehicles, and hundreds of different infantry units.
5.) Replay-ability: Tons of campaign story missions for all factions, which are well done for the most part. If you don't enjoy the story missions, or you finish them all, then the procedurally generated dynamic campaign (aka Conquest) game mode will keep you engrossed almost indefinitely. <This is personally what I play the most.

Cons: Of course no game is perfect. 
1.) The pathfinding for vehicles and soldiers can be frustratingly awful at times. The same can be said for issuing certain commands. Sometimes the soldiers/vehicles will straight up not do what you ask of them the first time. 
2.) The multiplayer co-op is not good. The UI for it is extremely laggy, and I think this has to do with the game's very old engine. (luckily most people aren't playing this game for the multiplayer co-op) 

TL;DR, this game is amazing. It's niche, but for anyone this game fills that niche for, it will be countless hours of fun. You can tell the developers behind this are very passionate about the game. I honestly didn't think it was possible to make a realistic WW2 RTS that didn't feel arcadey, but these guys actually did it. I highly recommend!

222617050.review:
GOH is a standout rts that requires a different approach to play than most other entries in the genre due to a very historically authentic focus. This can be great when you get a Tiger II to fight off waves off T-34 tanks, and maybe a little more stressful when you're commanding the T-34s, but its all in good fun if you're able to stomach some losses for the Motherland. Great pick up, especially on sale.

Pros

+ Historically authentic gameplay that uses combined arms tactics.
+ 3rd Person Direct Control that lets you take control of any soldier, tank, or gun, at any time.
+ 1000s of detailed vehicles, tanks, weapons and soldiers.
+ PTSD inducing sounds, effects and voice acting. You'll hear the flamethrower before you see it.
+ Boatloads of single-player, multiplayer, and user made content. Seriously, check out the steam workshop if you're on the fence, they've got 1980s, Star Wars, even Warhammer 40k conversion mods.
+ Dynamic campaign that lets you build a custom army.
+ High quality scripted campaign missions.
+ Consistent content updates, both DLC and free.
+ Great devs who are constantly communicating with the community, to the point that popular quality of life mods get incorporated as official updates.

Cons

- High price for the game and all DLCs. I'd recommend Finest Hour and Liberation as general pickups, Airborne if you like Band of Brothers, and the remainder if you're really a fan or Finnish.
- Some single player missions, particularly skirmish missions, are much lower quality than others. Any mission can be skipped, but it's still annoying to have taped bananas in between your Picasso's.
- Unique gameplay is great, but it means the first few hours of playtime will be a lot of learning and reloading.
- The skill floor for public matchmaking is very high.
- There's only so much graphics and effects can do about the underlying old game engine
- Pathfinding is very hit or miss, and when the misses get your tank blown up because it turned its side armor to an anti-tank gun well . . .

Pros

+ You can play for hundreds of hours and still lose (and still scapegoat the game)

222615322.review:
[h1] Fun but not yet fully polished [/h1]

This game was originally a DLC for a Modern Warfare type of [b][u] Call to Arms [/u][/b]; from my understanding, the DLC was so popular, the devs deciding to make a game based on the DLC; expanding it further into its own. As such, there is some "jank" and "clunk" to it at times but overall, the experience is awesome!

[h2] How does it compare? [/h2]
It's slower, more punishing, and more realistic than the [b] Company of Heroes [/b] franchise; yet faster, more intuitive, and familiar than the [b] Steel Division [/b] franchise. Infantry doesn't immediately get gunned down when pushing out into an open plain, but they aren't bullet sponges either. This game sits neatly besides the [b] Men of War [/b] franchise, however with more variety in units, game types, and even modding capabilities.

[h3] Detailed yet intuitive [/h3]
There are multiple layers to the gameplay however a gamers basic intuition may carry you through. Anti-tank infantry takes out tanks, flame throwers can burn down entire villages, artillery is devasting yet expensive, unwieldly, and vulnerable. Armor is devasting yet has poor visibility thus must be backed up with an Infantry presence and so on.

If you are at all a german panzer fan, soviet t34 fan, sherman fan, or even a british commonwealth enjoyer, you'll find unique units and interesting strategies that keep you engaged.
[u]Armored Combat[/u]
When fighting armored vehicles, you are not fighting a health bar. You are looking to get crew kills or module destruction. A destroyed turret/barrel means a tank has no way to punch back. A destroyed engine/tracks removes mobility. A tank with dead crew is potentionaly a new tank for you!

[h3] Ebb and Flow [/h3]
Multiplayer, Dynamic Conquest, and even Campaign offers a good back and forth dynamic within a given match. Matches/sessions lasting anywhere from 30 minutes to 1.5 hours, depending on your pace.
[u]Multiplayer[/u]
You essentially play a Deck of units based around specific play styles; Irregular, Offensive, Defensive, All-Arounder, and a few other options. You can do 1v1s up to I believe 4v4s I believe.

Due to the plethora of units, these matches take place in specific time periods; Early War, Mid War, and Late War. With each time period being pretty fun, my favorite being early war.

I believe there are 5 different game mode types.
[u]Dynamic Conquest[/u]
A persistent single player or cooperative game mode where you go against the AI; building and maintaining your "Deck" from scratch using manpower, research points, and ammunition. A lot of fun and is personally may preferred.

It's dynamic in the sense of whatever losses you incur, carry over through your campaign. If you have a Rifle Squad from your first mission that gets wiped on you third mission, it won't be available for your fourth mission.
[u] Campaign [/u]
It's, of course, railroaded but does a good job of introducing you to the mechanics of CTA. There are some cool missions to be enjoyed; I feel that are comparable and/or better than some of COH2s campaign missions.

[h1]Would recommend to friends, family, and your typical WW2 themed RTS enjoyer[/h1]

I really wanted to like this game. It looks like Company of Heroes, which is one of my favourite RTS games, but it just doesn’t feel the same in any way.

The learning curve is rough. You spend about 5 hours doing intro missions just to learn the basics, and even then it still doesn’t explain everything properly. When people tell you to go watch hours of YouTube just to understand the game, that’s a problem.

There’s way too much micromanagement. You can control soldiers in a few different ways, but it feels like that’s there to make up for bad AI and pathing. Units don’t behave well on their own, so you end up doing everything manually.

Some of the realism is cool, like how strong and long range tanks are. But the way the enemy acts with this realism is way off the mark. You can drive a tank right up to a soldier and then sit there waiting for the turret to slowly turn, while other soldiers stand nearby shooting it with rifles like it matters. Why aren't the soldiers running for their lives rather than just waiting for their turn for death? It just feels inconsistent.

Overall, it tries too hard to be realistic and forgets to be fun. If you’re expecting something like Company of Heroes, this isn’t it.

I don’t recommend it.

An incredibly detailed WWII RTS, verging on milsim in the level of micro you can get to. Practically speaking, however, this detail is either ignored or becomes a hindrance in large engagements (beyond even a single squad of infantry and one or two vehicles). 221606856.review:
For a -75% price, which it often is, I do recommend it.

It is one of those games similar to the Close Combat series and to the Syrian Warfare series. It could have been better than them, but has made some weird choices, like arcade-y maximum ranges (that are very hard to individually raise by editing, as many things need to be changed and the total max range is hard capped, so one would have to raise a general value first, and I don't know if that's possible,) that are very short. Also f.e. the Tiger Is armor has some sort of hitpoint system, that it is not impervious to smaller caliber fire. All artillery and mortar ranges are comically short.

The game lacks a simple Battle Maker, but has opted for the battle editor for modders, that is very difficult to use, or the constant combat mode, where the enemy always sees you and is scaling to what you do, making it annoying.

The campaigns also have been made with a weird choice to make the attack missions into a sort of "anti tank wall puzzles". What I mean by that is that you're going to be facing loads of AT and heavy AA guns and tanks and you're supposed to attack with just a few infantry in some sort of "Commandos" based gameplay, where your only option is to go 1st person Rambo, and "solve" the AT-wall puzzle from it's weak point onwards, as opposed to attacking with 3x vs 1x forces. This game play loop choice I think is a bad choice, as opposed to Close Combat and even Syrian Warfare series.

Why do I recommend it, then? Well, the units are very well made, both infantry and vehicles. The first mission I played was the German late war winter defense of the Panther-Wotan line (In Spite of Everything), and it was absolutely gorgeous. Just for that one mission the game is worth buying, but most of the defense missions are very fun to play. Sadly the attack missions are mostly against elevated AT and AA positions that you need to "solve" by zigzagging which you take out next in a Rambo fashion, or by sneaking about.

Buy the main game for -75% and see if you like it before buying the DLCs.

Call to Arms: Gates of Hell – My Guilty Pleasure of Chaos

I freaking love Gates of Hell. It’s WWII on steroids: brutal campaigns that make you sweat, squads that die faster than your patience in queue, and tanks that feel like angry metal rhinos. The single‑player campaigns are tense as hell — every mission feels like a “hold the line or get eaten” nightmare — and micromanaging soldiers is both a headache and an addictive power trip.

The AI sometimes goes rogue and the learning curve will punch you in the face, but the sound design, chaos, and insane modding community keep me coming back. Mods add new factions, missions, and tweaks that make every match feel fresh.

Pros: brutal realism, full control, epic chaos, mods for days
Cons: learning curve is savage, AI has mood swings, UI can be clunky

Verdict: I love this game. If you want hardcore tactical warfare, laugh at your own misfortunes, and dive into endless mods, this is an absolute must-play.

I enjoyed this game alot. 

If you like the Men of War series or enjoyed playing Company of Heroes with the Blitzkrieg-mod, this game is for you. I specifically recomend playing on the higher difficulties, as it really makes you think and plan ahead. A single mg is anough to mow down an infantry assault in the open, and tanks really are scary death-machines. 

Speak of tanks: The tank damage system is simliar to games like Warthunder, with the abilty to target the internals of the vehicle or directly kill infantry. I found that really cool, specifically because it is not something the more classic WW2 rts games did. 

If the is one point I would like to point out which may be a downer for some people: The micro in this game is really intense, sometime downright stupid for the amount of units you are expected to command. Units need resupply, fuel, repair and so on, which is fine enough. But it would be nice if units could automatically hop over fences and small walls, doing this in micro during an intense assault will get your guys killed. You can put the game on pause to give more complex commands, or chain commands using the shift key. But this also kills the flow of the game in my opinion. Tossing grenades and so on can also be a pain to manually do.

And another I really like: The ability to take command of individual units. This is so useful. Take command of critical units such as arty spotters, flame throwers and so on really enhances the your own assaults, making sure critical units do not f-up because of rts-typical bot behavior. Maning tanks and manually slogging out armour battles is also really nice. 

All in all: If you are a regular RTS player and love WW2 games, this game is an absolute must have!

220755365.review:
You see, I am really on the fence about this title. On one hand, historical accuracy and nerd content, cool models of everything, ballistics, penetration values, first-person view in RTS-game is cool as hell, true DEEP DYNAMIC CAMPAIGN FOR ANY FACTION etc. 

BUT. The direct control is the curse and the bless of this game simultaneously. AI in this game is notoriously bad at pathfinding, pretty much close to the first installation, Call to Arms, just a bit less dramatic. You can easily lose the whole convoy of vehicles which should've been running on designated via SHIFT key waypoints just because they dont give a ♥♥♥♥ about your waypoints, they have business of their own to attend.

Your vehicles and mortars accuracy is nerfed into the ground until you will possess this vehicle with your godlike essence and guide their weapons to the enemy's weakpoints. You can't really play this as a Blitzkrieg / Sudden Strike game, there is no really a choice between using and not using first-person view, it is a MUST. You can literally become one-man army with this feature or watch at your helpless tanks missing 75% of their shots. 

And don't even get me started on the infantry, it is just pain in the arse. They literally break their formation on the first possibility, they can change stance randomly, meeting artillery shells and MG fire with their brave but stupid broad chests. They can't even keep formation upon pressing attack movement, they just gather all at the pointing of your cursor lmao. Anyway, maybe that's a skill issue, but infantry management is clunky and requires an absurd APM. Also, they don't run from grenades automatically, they just stoically devour them and accept their martyrdom, no autonomy whatsoever. 

Anyway, if you accept this clunkiness, ready for intensive micromanagement and a lot of direct control, if you're a vet of Man of War series or just historical nerd - you will feel literally at home. If you expect this to play as modern Blitzkrieg but with cool graphics and true to history parameters - well, no such luck, it is entirely different game and it should be treated as such. 

Also, I must say I played with FoW on. I know that many people turn it off, making this game literally a shooting range, but what the point lol. I want strategy, not power fantasy about StuG soloing Battle for Sevastopol.

I can't really leave a negative review in good faith, cause it was really my expectations problem mostly, but I am disappointed. This game is simultaneously brilliant and outrageous. Definitely worth to try out, but not everyone will bear to stay with it long enough to truly enjoy Gates of Hell at its fullest.

When it comes to RTS games, Call to Arms: Gates of Hell feels like what you get when you take Company of Heroes 2 — already one of the better WWII strategy games — and turn everything up a notch.

There’s just a lot here. Mods, multiple game modes, and Dynamic Conquest, which almost feels like a roguelike with how each campaign plays out differently. The gameplay is deep and tactical, and you’ve got a lot of freedom in how you approach fights. It’s the kind of game where you’re still learning new things dozens of hours in.

The only real downside is the price. With all the DLC, it’s not cheap. But since a friend gifted it to me for Christmas, I can’t really complain.

There’s plenty to learn, and it’s easy to sink serious time into it. The 100 euros it cost with all the DLC on sale has already paid off for me — and I’m pretty sure it’ll pay off several times over.

Not the easiest RTS to get into, but definitely one of the most rewarding.

219372336.review:
As an avid WWII buff and longtime RTS player, Call to Arms: Gates of Hell – Ostfront should be exactly my kind of game.

In many ways, it is.

The visuals are strong. The historical accuracy of the war machines and units is impressive. The sound design — from small arms to Sherman engines to heavy artillery — does a fantastic job immersing you in the battlefield. When artillery starts landing, it feels right. Atmosphere and authenticity are not the problem here.

Which makes the shortcomings even more frustrating.

Campaign Missions
You’re locked into using whatever units the mission gives you, with little to no freedom in composition or reinforcements. I understand the realism — in war you use what you’re given — but realism doesn’t always equal fun.

Skirmish is better. You capture territory, unlock reinforcements over time, and choose what to bring in. That’s where the game feels the most alive. The problem is you only ever unlock a small slice of the total roster. The game includes everything from scout tanks to super-heavies, yet you rarely get to use most of them. And once you finally unlock the “good stuff,” the mission ends because you’ve captured everything.

Just when it gets interesting — it’s over.

Conquest Mode is where the game almost becomes incredible. You earn resources, unlock units at your discretion, and deploy them in point-limited waves. On paper, it’s perfect.

In practice, it becomes repetitive. There are only two mission types: attack or defend. Attack missions are straightforward and fine. Defense missions, however, can take 45–60 minutes of holding points while a slow counter fills. I enjoy the occasional wave defense. I don’t enjoy doing it constantly. It becomes tedious to the point where I sometimes auto-lose just to move on.

The campaign “map” is also just a web of lines between missions. There’s no actual front line, no sense of choosing where you fight. One mission is hedgerows, the next is winter snow, with no geographic logic tying it together.

UI clarity is another small but noticeable issue. When playing as the Germans, unit unlocks are labeled in German with little explanation, so unless you already know what you’re looking at, you’re unlocking blindly.

This game falls into what I call the “98% category.”

The realism is excellent.
The detail is excellent.
The sound and atmosphere are excellent.
The core mechanics are strong.

But that last 2% — mission design, pacing, variety, and UI clarity — is what determines whether it’s actually fun to play long-term.

It’s not a bad game.

It’s a frustratingly close-to-great game.

i really want to like this game. i've always wanted something a little more than CoH2 after sinking hundreds of hours into that game and came across this which at first glance looked like a gem. it clearly has a lot of love and labor put into it. there are hundreds of detailed, historically accurate models of vehicles and other things from several nations and the terrain and building destruction is beautiful, but there is ultra autism levels of tedious micromanagement that is not at all fun to interact with. you will have no fun micromanaging, and you will have no fun not micromanaging, because the game will punish you and all your troops will be fist-****ed and killed.

after i finished the tutorials, i tried the very first german campaign mission several times and got absolutely pounded each time. ok, fair enough, i'm new so maybe i'm not getting something. so on my last run, i meticulously babysat the braindead infantry, micromanaged the light arty to bombard hardpoints without getting instantly gibbed by invisible AT guns, and flanked and assaulted with tanks through direct control (which honestly feels like the only fair way to play this game.) this took me almost an hour in real life, and after clearing the two objectives with some losses i figured i finally had beaten this campaign mission and had extrapolated maybe a bit of fun until the next part of the mission started and the map doubled in size with new enemy hardpoints. i thought i'd humor myself and threw a couple more tanks at the enemy but eventually grew sick and tired of this mission so i ragequit.

i love strategy games and can appreciate a drawn out dramatic brawl of attrition but the difference in most other games is that i am not micromanaging each nanosecond like GoH. if i let up the micromanaging at any second in combat my units are going to be eviscarated because the TTK in this game is essentially real life. even staying on top of micromanaging you will be fisted at times because your infantry stop and stand still for a second each time you change their movement orders and then take a bullet to the noggin.

i figured campaign wasnt for me and tried conquest. the first attack mission was fun enough, i direct controlled a tank (i spec'd all my research into the strongest one i could afford because i wanted to eventually work up to a tiger) and slaughtered all i saw and captured the points. moving on to the defense segment, i was appalled to see i had to defend TWO points at once as if the micromanaging wasn't bad enough for one objective (granted, there's inherently less movement-micromanaging for defending).

long story short, i kept direct control of my tank again to try and cut down on the enemy size as much as i could before they would reach my points and my defending infantry. unfortunately i was instantly tracked and then destroyed by an AT gun in the forest somewhere, and thus the run was instantly dead after 10 minutes of preparation. skill issue or whatever.

nonetheless, this game is just not fun for the vast majority of people, myself included. i tried to keep an open mind, i watched youtube videos and tried to pay attention to how people moved their troops, i searched on reddit and steam for tips on how to get better, i played on my own for several hours to see if i would get the feel of the game, but there is just no solution to the inherent flaw of the constant micromanaging and it gets exponentially worse the larger yours and the enemy's army gets and the increasingly powerful units they throw at you.

this kind of franchise was built for one squadron to be actively micromanaged, which wasn't bad. but the scale of these games have increased dramatically and the mechanics have had almost no innovation, OR, they've had innovation towards even more micromanagement (the inventory system). the inventory is abysmal. spending 10 minutes fiddling back and forth between inventories in the tutorial to fill up a tank was a terrible experience. and this was in a lull when all the enemies are dead, do the devs really expect people to **** with the inventory system in a massive battle and have any success doing so?

i wish that AI in this game was improved as a whole and there were more inclusions of allied AI in conquest which is really the only mode that i can muster up some enjoyment in. in conquest defense, i wish there were some allied soldiers pre-placed in defensive positions on your points and you would just need a few moments to fill in the gaps with your own troops and incorporate some AT and MG. i wish you could call in AI reinforcements in both defense and attack, who would move around and engage the enemy at their own discretion while you worry about maybe at most a couple squadrons of your own soldiers. i exclusively play CoH2 PVE with a couple AI allies for this reason so the battle feels more dynamic and everything is not always resting on my shoulders. i don't have to worry about skipping around the map every 2 seconds and precisely moving troops back, forward, or side to side so they don't die in a milisecond because they're an inch out of place, and i can accept more easily when i actually do need to micromanage a little for a particular coordinated push with say armor and infantry.

again, CoH2 nailed a good balance. while Ostfront and games before it (Men of War Assault Squad 2) go absolutely overkill and increase the size and amount of squadrons you are managing at any given time AND the complexity of the individual units themselves by granting them less autonomy and incorporating layers upon layers of interaction with things like stances, inventories, holstering weapons (WHY?), etc. CoH2 had manageable numbers of squadrons, and an acceptable complexity to each. the TTK was also not literally real-life like Ostfront giving you much more time to react and adapt to a unit that may have been ambushed or accidentally overextended rather than having it be a complete and utter loss while you were busy managing 20 other units like Ostfront.

also, DLC prices are too steep, and as a previous reviewer Booba put it perfectly:
"Players (who don't abuse prescription amphetamines) are over-saturated with tasks, to the point that it's easier to complete a mission by playing the game like War Thunder or an awful third person shooter than it is to actually command troops."

tl;dr: seemingly high quality and decent game, suffering from the inherent unfun micromanaging flaw all games of this franchise have with no innovation to address it. this is a niche game that has its moments and from what i can see has a strong and loving community but in its current state it is too annoying and frusturating to play and cannot properly be enjoyed by the vast majority of people.

The latest offering from the digital ghetto, masquerading under the title *Call to Arms: Gates of Hell – Ostfront*, presents itself as a simulation of history’s most profound catastrophe. Yet, like the culture industry’s endless stream of identical trinkets, it merely replicates the very barbarism it purports to represent, selling the horror of the Eastern Front as a consumable entertainment. It is a reified nightmare, packaged for the masses.

The initial encounter with its cumbersome user interface is a lesson in bureaucratic frustration. One does not so much command a unit as negotiate with a hostile and unyielding administrative apparatus. The menus, a labyrinth of poor design, stand as an insurmountable barrier between the player and any semblance of unmediated experience. This is not play; it is labor, a tedious exercise in navigating a system designed by engineers who have mistaken opacity for depth.

The game’s structure, particularly its brutal difficulty curve, reflects the very irrationality of the historical processes it trivializes. The challenge is not a product of strategic depth, but of an arbitrary and unbalanced cruelty. This is most evident in the multiplayer mode, a space ostensibly for social interaction, yet rendered a totalizing experience by the inability to save progress. Here, the game demands a false commitment, a surrender to its chaotic and often broken logic, mocking any hope of considered, reflective action. The player is trapped in a perpetual, grinding present, unable to learn or correct course.

This "Ostfront" is, of course, a thinly veiled replica of the *Men of War* series. The similarities are not mere influence but a symptom of the culture industry’s standardization. It is the same product, the same gameplay loop, simply repainted with new icons and a fresh veneer of pixels, sold back to a consumer base too pacified to demand true innovation. The genre has become a museum of itself, displaying only corpses.

The game’s one advertised feature, the granular control over individual soldiers, is perhaps its most damning indictment. The player is reduced to a micro-manager, a puppeteer of digital flesh, obsessively clicking to adjust the angle of a rifle or the trajectory of a thrown grenade. This fetishization of minute detail offers not a connection to the individual soldier’s experience, but a complete alienation from it. The soldier becomes a pure object, a collection of data points to be manipulated. In the end, *Gates of Hell* offers only the semblance of agency, a detailed control panel for a vehicle racing blindly toward an abyss of its own making.

7/10

I captured a BT-5, rearmed it and refueled it.  I then told the tank to drive left.  The AI decided to drive forward and to the right instead: into the fuel truck.  The resulting explosion killed the tank's gunner, wounded the driver and killed half of the squad of infantry, who were standing nearby.

Hell of a tutorial.  I don't think "our pathfinding sucks, watch out" was technically part of the curriculum, but they nailed that lesson across multiple tutorial missions anyway.  I'd refund if I could, but I can't, and a thug of a forum moderator thinks it's a good idea to delete threads criticizing their game, so I'm just going to write an unhappy review instead.

Even if its pathfinding wasn't so atrocious, Gates of Hell: Ostfront suffers from the same problem most RTS games do these days: not enough strategy, and too much micromanagement.  It's a game of whack-a-mole with multiple boards, specialized hammers, and specialized moles that break certain hammers.  These are twitch-skill games, requiring players to micromanage dozens of things simultaneously.  Players (who don't abuse prescription amphetamines) are over-saturated with tasks, to the point that it's easier to complete a mission by playing the game like War Thunder or an awful third person shooter than it is to actually command troops.

It's a shame.  RTS games have always been one of my favorite genres, but at their core, they haven't changed much from the WarCraft and Command and Conquer days.  "Stand and shoot" is [i]still[/i] the only thing your little dudes can be relied upon to do.

218811508.review:
Game is fun, though it can definitely piss you off sometimes.

What hooked me:
The shell penetration system is surprisingly deep. Vehicles don’t just explode when you “have enough armor penetration.” You have to account for projectile angle, vehicle positioning, armor thickness at different spots, and more. When you finally land a clean shot and a tank blows up in a fiery explosion, it’s quite satisfying.

Immersion & Tension:
The atmosphere is dark and heavy, especially with fog of war enabled. On larger maps, sending a scout for intel is crucial, getting flanked can be brutal. It adds a real sense of strategy and immersion.

Teamplay & Multiplayer:
The game really shines with co-op or multiplayer. Solo is fine, but coordinating with teammates is where the depth shows. Different players often run complementary doctrines, help each other’s fronts, or send reinforcements strategically. PvP is also an option if that’s more your style.

Gameplay & Strategy:
You can’t play braindead here. You need to carefully manage units, equipment choice, and doctrine. Different doctrines and playstyles drastically change how battles flow, which keeps things fresh and tactical. If you’re new to RTS games, Ostfront will likely take a bit to learn.

Downsides:

Uses player-hosted matches instead of dedicated servers which can cause lag for geographically distant friends.

AI can sometimes be dumb, buggy, or slow. Not constant, but noticeable at times.

Verdict:
Immersive, tactical, and more intense than it looks at first glance. If you like slower, methodical WW2 RTS games, Ostfront is definitely worth trying.

TL;DR:
Fun and immersive WW2 RTS with realistic armor penetration that makes positioning and angling matter. Multiplayer is where it really shines thanks to teamwork and doctrine variety. Downsides: player-hosted servers can lag, AI can be buggy. New RTS players should expect a learning curve.

After just finishing the German Ostfront campaign and with almost 200 hours in the game, I think I can give an accurate review of this amazing game.  

Firstly, this game requires the most learning, practice, and experimentation of almost anything I have ever played.  There are undocumented control combos and other features that you pick up from playing that turn out to be crucial for success.  You do have to intensely micro a lot in this game but you have both the ability to slow time and pause.  Slowing time is almost mandatory for an effective defensive.  Prepare to push through the frustration. 

Secondly, you need a lot of time to play most missions.  Spending over four hours on a mission is not uncommon if you are going to explore all the things the developers include in it to make it unique and fun (i.e. supply caches, abandoned working vehicles, secondary objectives, etc.).  The campaign missions are so intense you are actually exhausted when some of them are done.

But if you put in the time and effort, this is the game you were always hoping that Close Combat, Combat Mission, and every other tactical WW2 game you ever played would be like.  The sound, animations, and effects are just insane.  You know when an 88 fires just behind you.  Destructible environments add realism and strategies to the mix.  Also, the environments, uniforms, and vehicles are so beautiful and varied I actually pause and put the camera in cinematic viewpoints to just marvel at it all.  Finally, the supply, fuel, repair logistics alone can keep you busy if you want to let your unit AI fight it out but make sure they have what they need to survive and conquer.

For the reasonable price for the base game, and the amount you get for each DLC, this game is steal for your entertainment dollar.  If you pick them all up in a Steam sale, its a no brainer.

If you love Company of Heroes, this is the next level.

I’ve been playing Company of Heroes for many years, and it has always been one of my favorite RTS games. But in January, I discovered Call to Arms: Gates of Hell – Ostfront, and honestly… this is exactly the game I was looking for.

I still enjoy Company of Heroes a lot, but Gates of Hell is on a completely different level.

The biggest difference is the amount of control you have. You’re not locked into rigid unit behavior, you can select individual soldiers and assign them specific tasks. This makes every battle feel far more tactical and personal. On top of that, you constantly have to supply your units with ammunition, fuel, and other resources, nothing is unlimited. Logistics play a huge role, and that adds a lot of depth to every battle.

One of the absolute highlights is the First Person mode. Being able to jump directly into a soldier or vehicle during a battle is incredible and adds an immersion you rarely see in RTS games.

The game rewards planning, awareness, and realism. Flanking matters, logistics matter, and mistakes are punished, but in a fair and satisfying way. The scale of battles, the physics, the destructible environments, and the attention to detail are outstanding. Mods and ongoing updates also add tons of replay value.

In short:
If you love Company of Heroes, this game is an absolute must-play. It goes much deeper, offers far more freedom, and delivers a more immersive and realistic WWII experience.

Highly recommended.

This game has reshaped how I experience gaming as a medium. Like many players, I came in with a deep appreciation for history, and the development team has delivered an experience that remains largely faithful to real events. What elevates the game from simply good to genuinely memorable is its tailored realism. The world feels familiar enough that players can intuitively “read” situations, deciding how to approach objectives without relying on rigid rules.

There is no single way to win, only an objective to take and the units available to do so. How players employ those tools reflects their own critical thinking, turning each engagement into a test of judgment rather than reflexes. Sadly, the game has natural limitations, the AI can only go so far, and online play can feel intimidating for many, myself included. Still, few games have held my attention the way this one has, and i'm sure everyone can relate to their first moment trying to disable a KV-1 with insufficient firepower.

At times the experience feels unbalanced, but that imbalance is intentional. It forces adaptation and problem-solving in a way few games attempt. While I wish the developers leaned further into the extreme asymmetry present in certain periods of the war, (!more unbalance please!). The current design strikes a workable middle ground between balance and realism for online and single play, capturing the tension of fighting against overwhelming odds at times and feeling like a steamroller in others.

216864181.review:
★★★★★ The most mechanically deep WWII RTS currently available

After 379+ hours, Call to Arms: Gates of Hell – Ostfront stands as the most technically advanced and system-driven WWII RTS on the market.

The simulation depth is exceptional. Units are modeled with historically accurate parameters including armor layout, shell types, penetration mechanics, effective engagement ranges, reload times, crew behavior, and component-level vehicle damage. Armor combat is resolved through real ballistic interaction rather than abstract hit points, making positioning, angling, and target discipline decisive.

Infantry combat is equally nuanced. Suppression, stamina, cover quality, line-of-sight, and terrain elevation all materially influence outcomes. Fire superiority, overlapping fields of fire, and terrain control matter far more than raw unit numbers.

The hybrid RTS plus direct control system is where the game truly excels. Manual weapon control, vehicle handling, and moment-to-moment intervention allow skilled players to shape engagements without turning the experience into an APM race. Tactical execution consistently outweighs macro optimization.

The AI performs credibly, particularly in defensive behavior, flanking attempts, and combined-arms usage. While not flawless, it provides meaningful opposition rather than scripted pressure.

Visually, the game continues to hold up very well. Terrain deformation, destruction modeling, and battlefield readability remain impressive given the simulation running underneath.

Mod support and replayability are outstanding, with community content often rivaling official expansions in depth and scope.

This is not a casual RTS. It rewards patience, battlefield awareness, and doctrinal thinking. In return, it delivers engagements that feel organic, unscripted, and earned.

⸻

Wishlist / Potential Enhancements

While the game already models combat at an unusually deep level, several historically significant elements of German military doctrine are still missing or only partially represented:

• Camouflage and concealment systems
A proper camouflage mechanic would greatly enhance realism. The German army invested heavily in concealment, including field-applied camouflage, foliage integration, camo nets, and specialized uniform patterns. Units should be able to actively camouflage when stationary, with detection influenced by movement, distance, optics quality, and observer experience.

• Camouflage nets for vehicles and static weapons
Historically widespread yet currently absent. Deployable camouflage nets for anti-tank guns, artillery, and parked vehicles would add meaningful defensive gameplay and encourage prepared positions rather than constant mobility.

• Improved ambush and deception mechanics
German doctrine strongly emphasized ambush tactics, delayed engagement, and positional deception. Systems allowing units to remain hidden until firing, simulate false positions, or benefit from first-shot bonuses would reflect this more accurately.

• Doctrinal differences in command philosophy
Mission-type tactics (Auftragstaktik) were central to German operations. A lightweight system where veteran units operate more independently, react faster, or retain cohesion under loss of command would add historical flavor without excessive micromanagement.

• Crew experience affecting vehicle effectiveness more strongly
German emphasis on trained crews was decisive, especially in armored warfare. More pronounced differences in reload speed, target acquisition, and damage control based on crew quality would deepen vehicle combat even further.

• Field fortification depth
While basic entrenchment exists, historically accurate options like improved foxholes, revetments, and prepared firing positions would further support defensive playstyles.

⸻

Even without these features, Gates of Hell – Ostfront already stands at the top of its genre. With additions like these, it could move from being an exceptional RTS to a near-authentic real-time battlefield simulation.

Five stars. Still playing far too much — and still discovering new tactical possibilities.

It's a RTT/RTS where you can play it as a first person shooter if you want. You can click a unit and right click somewhere to move it there, or press E to direct control it. This gives you top down control of the unit. If you want third person shooter view you press T and then you can play that way. You can loot enemy corpses and repair their vehicles for your own use if that's your thing.

You get access to many units, for example you can direct control infantry, tanks, half tracks, armored cars, trucks, and even a ship in one mission. There are many different kinds of infantry and vehicles you get access to. In some missions you can call for artillery or air support, but you can't control planes. Enemy planes can be tough to shoot down in the heat of the moment. Sometimes artillery isn't off-screen like when you capture enemy artillery and use it against them.

The game is realistic-style. (For example, cool as it would be, they wouldn't add ship-boarding or parachuting because of the realism constraint.) Vehicles are modeled so shooting them in specific spots deals specific types of damage. But the vehicle weapons/artillery have shorter ranges than they would have in real life. (So that it's close quarters and more fun)

Sometimes the bots navigate things weird or get stuck on obstacles and you might not notice it.
The campaign can also be quite hard especially if the enemy has lots of firepower. Luckily there is the save feature that lets you reset to earlier points when you were doing well.
Landmines can be very BS to deal with, but if you stick to the roads you should be fine. On the flip side, laying mines and using AT obstacles is a really strong way for you to defend.
There can also be frustrating moments where you can't get a vehicle to work even though it is perfectly fine, because it has 0 fuel (like if the fuel tank was ruptured earlier).
Enemy infantry can also be bullet sponges, but explosives deal with them quite well.
Campaign missions can take a long time to do. But you can use save feature to break it into manageable chunks.

Overall the game is recommended for those who like the realistic-style RTT/third person shooter hybrid with some adjustments made to make it more fun.

Good game; hostile developers.

TL;DR the game is great if you enjoy the idea of a WWII-era sandbox and are curious about how RTS and direct-control action can come together in a SP/MP Co-op or PvP experience. The game is actively being worked on and often comes on sale as a set. It also features full campaign co-op and various other skirmish-type game modes, and PvP/PvE. I recommend it for the gameplay, especially if you want to co-op it with a friend.

But the only time I've dealt with the devs, (which I didn't even know until someone clarified), I have to say I was very bitterly disappointed with the attitudes and lack of basic respect I saw. More on that below.


So this is the first and only game of the Gem engine I have any experience with. I own and have played no Men of War games prior. This incident started out by my making a polite suggestion that some sort of test/practice range or mode could be introduced. The reason is that the game has a myriad of weapons/vehicles in it (flamethrowers, rockets, cannons, various shell types, direct fire, indirect fire, etc.) that you will largely only get to use in the moment of action.

While much of how xyz is used is clear to history nerds, there's still a lot of nuance that can only be sussed out by trial. After all, that is the whole point of direct-control being in the game, with human-controlled units fairly likely to outperform computer-controlled ones.

Presently, "testing" can only be done by: learning the editor and setting up an entire custom scenario, practicing against bots, or somewhat cantankerously setting up a skirmish mission, toggling off the enemy AI, and essentially enabling a test (free spawns) mode. The first can be done by following youtube tutorials, the second is exactly what one wants to avoid, and the third works well enough but is messy, as you can't really de-spawn anything once spawned (gets crowded fast), and you will still have a time limit set by the scenario. None of these solutions are ideal, which is why the suggestion was made. Not just a practice range to test weapons, but also to test specific units v. other units, and to see for instance first-hand how big a difference various proficiencies make as well with unit veterancy. Doing so whilst being able to clear up trash and de-spawn units would be great. Moreover, because in Skirmish mode, (the replayable custom mode) you are only able to choose specific "doctrines" which determine what units you can bring that fit a certain tactical role, so an entire faction's roster is usually not available to you using the test mode.

What I was told, rather dismissively, was that "This can be done already (with the editor)", and a starting tutorial of the editor was shared. My point, though, was not that I can learn the engine's editor and set up some particular scenario. No particular scenario would cover every possible setup, and that wasn't the aim of my suggestion, but the idea rather was that the game could include an option with its own built-in test range where you can choose the equipment from any faction, toggle on/off AI, clear the debris, etc. It'd be the ultimate basic testing ground, without a time limit or mission-related limitations.

I was criticized and more or less berated for bothering to waste time making a suggestion and to argue in favor of this concept, instead of learning how to use their engine's built-in scenario editor to "do it myself" as the original response demanded. Only MUCH later into the conversation was it let slip that the engine could not actually do this; something about specific factions and doctrines being tied directly to the spawned map or scenario. In other words, you couldn't spawn a particular map with just any unit from any faction/doctrine, but would have to essentially start/restart the scenario with particular sets in mind to be able to spawn them. Something like that. Which would explain why Skirmish includes the "Test" mode toggle in the first place, despite it essentially being an aberration of the Skirmish mode itself, still including a time limit, still including visible objectives, etc.

Now, if an engine limitation is hard-coded that disallows a universal test range concept to be developed, that is completely understandable. Hard engine limitations are what they are, and no one is expecting magic. But it would have been far more professional and respectful if someone stated, "Hey, (first of all) developer here. Engine limitations prevent a mode where any materiel can be spawned in cross-factions and cross-doctrines. You can try Skirmish mode without enemy AI and enabling 'test' mode as a sandbox, or you can try to set up a custom scenario using our editor. Here is a link for a tutorial: (link)." 

Instead, rather dismissively, I was told, "You can already do this", and when I simply argued that the player having to learn the engine's editor and setting up their own scenario was not ideal, and misses the point, I was berated for wasting so much time pushing for a concept instead of learning to use their editor. Referring to the test mode, I was told something along the lines of, "That seems a solution suited to your abilities given you seem to refuse to want to learn the editor", implying I was an idiot or irrationally stubborn by thinking the suggestion reasonable. It wasn't even until later on that someone in passing clarified that the original response was posted by a developer. So only after the condescension and insult was it made clear that it was essentially the message of the devs that such a notion just wasn't possible, and thus not worth suggesting.

Here's the rub. I'm not an idiot. And if I care to make a suggestion about a game I've paid for, it's usually well thought-out. Moreover this idea isn't insane or unreasonable, TONS of games do have practice/test range types of scenarios. Strategy/command-type games, as far as I know, a little less so. But I've dealt with editors since Age of Empires II, and editors in modern games like Arma 3, and in terms of getting from nothing to a spawned stage with a unit from one faction versus a unit from another and then actively testing it, I find both of those more initially straight-forward and logical than the editor I saw when I opened it.

Now again, my point to clarify is not that "this is hard", it is that having to go through these hoops to test out specific equipment is clunky, and not user-friendly. (If your game requires me to watch a youtube tutorial for such a basic aspect, I consider that a flaw.) And I do not consider any of the editors I've used ever to be especially user-friendly; in other words I would not expect any of them to be ideal solutions for a built-in, user-friendly universal testing ground. A world exists where Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront is a game that could quite benefit from a quick, simple, universal testing ground, while also being true that the engine simply does not support that. That is A-Okay! But to be condescended to and disparaged by the developers themselves for making a fairly ordinary suggestion is pretty wild. I expect it from any particular gaming community to have some rude members, but I expected more decorum from developers.

For what it's worth, I am not alone either. Someone else in the thread even thought it was a good idea and joked about, "I don't know why you're getting such flak for this". Moreover, somewhat similar notions exist, as you can see here: https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3155552868 So rather than trying to force a clunky editor down your player's throats and condescending them for not learning it, leading with engine limitations and the (only?) possible solutions makes a lot more sense for someone whose money you have accepted for the product.

216538806.review:
Call to Arms: Gates of Hell is an excellent real-time tactics game set during the Second World War. It traces its lineage back to heavily modded Men of War: Assault Squad 2, but this is a bold and effective evolution of that formula. The atmosphere is noticeably darker and more grounded, with the arcade, shoot-’em-up feel of Men of War largely rejected in favour of a more hardcore, realism-focused approach.

Units can be controlled directly in third person, allowing for granular micro-management when needed, but the game truly shines when you engage with it as a tactical commander rather than a lone gunman.

The base game focuses on the Eastern Front, but several DLCs expand the scope to include the Western Front, and Northern Front, introducing US and Commonwealth forces, and Finnish forces, respectively, and their associated equipment and doctrine.

There is also a strong modding scene. Notably, the popular Valour mod significantly broadens the game’s scope, adding factions, units, weapons, vehicles, and even entirely new theatres and eras, including Imperial Japanese forces and Pacific-theatre assets for use in Conquest mode.

If Company of Heroes or Men of War has begun to feel too gamey, repetitive, or arcade-oriented, Gates of Hell takes the core ideas of the Men of War formula and refines them into a far more authentic and immersive depiction of battlefield tactics.

Highly recommended to fans of tactical command games, whether your background is Men of War, Total War, or any similar strategy title that rewards patience, positioning, and realism.

Gates of Hell is now in a state where I can confidently say that this game is worth buying. Aesthetically, the game is beautiful and it is much more stable for a GEM2 engine game. There is plenty of content available for the base game alone and various gamemodes make a return from the old Men of War style combat zones to new ones such as dynamic campaign.

New assets are a welcome site after previous Men of War titles rehashing the same voice lines, unit models, and textures over and over again. Moreover, the campaigns are a vast improvement as they include both the original Faces of War style missions as well as Assault Squad skirmish style too.

The quality of playable content itself can vary and it is clear that different teams have worked on different projects as various missions have noticeable bugs and scripting errors - this goes the same for DLC too. Furthermore, it is a shame that there is a lack of GUI scaling (particularly lack of 4K support) considering this is a modern title and should have modern standards.

Personally, I play this game for it's sandbox content where I can create my own projects and share with the growing Gates of Hell community on the workshop. There is also a strong multiplayer scene although I am not much into playing online myself.

As this is one of the later releases of a game using the GEM2 engine, it is regularly updated, hotfixed, and patched by the developers and they do indeed listen to community feedback. However, I cannot justify the game's pricing if you want to play other WW2 factions, such as the United States, Commonwealth, Finland, and access to other units. It is not pay to win, but for a game about WW2 factions and locking the player to essentially only the Soviet Union and a limited German roster is outrageous.

My advice would be to either download mods from the workshop, such as 'Valour' to play as any faction you want for free, or buy this game plus it's DLC when a Steam sale occurs. Otherwise I simply cannot justify 'Total War WARHAMMER style' pricing.

Overall, I highly recommend this title as it is the latest iteration of the WW2 RTS on the GEM2 engine with 64-bit support and amazing overall asset quality despite it's shortcomings in mission quality and pricing. I hope to see more from BarbedWireStudios in the future!

UPDATE: After giving the game a lot more time, I can say one thing very confidently — the original German and Soviet campaign missions (and some of the Finnish DLC ones) are legitimately terribly designed, and the dev never bothered to fix them. When you try the US DLC missions, or the later German / Soviet DLC, it's clear that the dev took far more time figuring out how to avoid game-breaking mission mechanics and "insta-fail" scenarios out of the player's control. 

E.g., in one original mission, you're asked to protect a convoy of trucks which you have no control over the pathing of, and then proceed to go get insta-KOed because they drive onto a high road AHEAD OF THE FRONT LINE. Completely absurd mission scripting that just serves to punish the player. 

Most of the small-squad "stealth" missions are also... garbage. You can see they wanted this to scale down to a 3rd-person "squad tactics" action game early on in development, and were later forced to abandon certain playstyles because they just weren't fun or practical. This game is fun when you're in a medium-scale assault or defense scenario, but is a tedious and unrewarding slog when you're microing 5-10 guys across a map. Similarly, the game only scales upward so well — scenarios with more than 10 tanks / AT assets on the map at a given moment simply turn into pileups once you learn how to position your anti-armor, because the AI just keeps making predictable mistakes.

Tl;dr, a lot of missions are terrible (and you will probably skip 50-60% of them; many are just not fun). The good misisons are legitimately fun, unit pathing is very broken, and artillery + snipers are tremendously OP.

ORIGINAL REVIEW: A game that fuses the best of Combat Mission and the worst of Company of Heroes and World of Tanks. Wants to be everything -- a real-time squad tactics game, a place-and-spawn RTS, and a weird 3rd-person action sim. In the end, CTA Gates of Hell ends up being great at none of them, and mediocre to bad at all.

Yes, it has a massive library of historic vehicles and weapons. Yes, the unit animations and sound effects are pretty cool. And yes, you can create your own scenarios and play out historic battles like you're running your own little cinematic board game. And that's exactly who this game is for: WWII tactics board game nerds.

The unit pathing is awful, especially for vehicles. Mission scripting is horrible, half the time you have no idea what you're supposed to be doing. The voice acting is the among the most amateur hour stuff I've seen in a modern video game. 

But the worst part of this game is easily the infantry / armor / AT balance. The developers plainly never figured out how to integrate AT / field guns in a way that wouldn't make them tremendously OP (i.e., knocking out tanks under every circumstance), so their solution is to make them extremely fragile and prone to getting one-shotted by tanks. This completely breaks many of the single player missions, where you as the defending force have two, maybe three AT guns on the field with extremely limited viable options for placement, and no ability to replace them. The AI gets lucky and pops one or both of your AT guns halfway through the mission? As happens CONSTANTLY as the Soviets and Finns? You just need to restart the mission; it's game over. Infantry are hopeless at antitank, and won't reliably throw AT grenades (... or run in a remotely logical way when ordered to throw one) when tanks get near.

When everything "works" right, this game can be fun. But that's so rarely the case. And the moments when you do need to take manual control of your units simply aren't very rewarding -- it's typically because you have a tank or AT gun that target hunts to the point that it won't fire at anything (and so it about to get annihilated).

Good concept, poor execution. Pretty sure I'm giving up on this game.

Call to Arms: Gates of Hell is easily my favorite RTT/RTS game and might be my favorite World War II game of all time. It has the best dynamic damage system with it's vehicles, as well as a crazy attention to detail, and those things are really what sold me on this game.

Knocking out an enemy tiger, securing the area, fixing the tiger, crewing it with a bunch of Russian penal riflemen who ran out of ammo and using it to brutalize the German front lines has got to be one of the coolest things you can do in a game.  However, this game is riddled with bugs that have not been fixed since the game was released.

These bugs range from slightly annoying, to game breaking. This being said, I have not experienced any crashes yet. These bugs include but are not limited to: Your unit completely ignoring move orders, Your unit getting stuck on the environment (This is especially bad with artillery pieces), Your unit getting stuck in an infinite loop equipping their firearm (This makes them useless), And in 3rd person direct control mode your units like to randomly forget how to pull a trigger (The firearm/cannon won't shoot no matter how many times you left click, this happens with infantry and vehicles). There are many, many more examples I'm either forgetting or omitting for the sake of brevity. 

This game is great, so great, I just wish the devs would spend a little more time fixing the old bugs that have haunted longtime players like me, instead of releasing more DLC bug fixes that don't fix long standing underlying problems.

If you like RTS games or WW2, buy this game and play this game. But buy it on sale, because I don't see these bugs being fixed within my lifetime. Play conquest mode after you get done with the campaigns, use direct control mode often.

(Additional notes) Please make the liberated nations mod vanilla, This mod makes it to where you can fight against anyone as anyone in conquest. It adds so much more to do in conquest and makes for some super interesting ahistorical gameplay. Not sure why this wasn't implemented when the game first released but it needs to be added to the game along with the long awaited bug fixes I've already mentioned, there are also some issues with artillery and tanks being too indecisive with their targets, swapping between AP and HE shells instead of firing on targets because they see infantry and tanks and get confused. 

Also, sometimes artillery and tanks will continue to fire on vehicles that have already been knocked out and that I may want to repair. Also also, please make a prototype tank DLC for each nation, for use in conquest and multiplayer optionally.

Time is very important in this game and when every third order you give is ignored and your unit's AI pales in comparison to the superior Ubermensch AI, it makes things a lot less fun and a lot more frustrating.

212621628.review:
After playing for approximately 100 hours at this point and completing a large majority of the campaigns with plenty still to go, I think it's a good time to review. I have purchased all the DLCs for GoH although the base game stuff is still really great. If you're looking for something more in depth than Company of Heroes this is your place. Your units need to be supplied and can run out of ammo. The inventory system is very interesting but can get finnicky at times. There can be extreme challenge in this game. It comes with a fair share of frustrations. Despite so I think this is the WW2 strategy game to have. If you want to just focus on commanding units you can or if you want a more personal touch you can direct control units. This is especially useful for your emplacements, vehicles or if you just need that pinpoint AT shot. The details of the units and vehicles are very well done.

  For missions/content for the base game you have a tutorial (played as the Germans), a Soviet campaign and German campaign. There is also a free content pack that adds 3 more missions (Jubilee). There are skirmishes incorporated which are essentially you starting on one side of the map and having to progress and capture points that give you better units. The DLC add more nations and campaigns such as the U.S Liberation and U.S Airborne (U.S.) [Liberation also gives you a German campaign for the Western Front], Talvisota (Finnish), The newest, Finest Hour (Commonwealth and German of early war). Scorched Earth adds more missions into the original German and Soviet campaigns.

  The Conquest mode (Dynamic Campaign) lets you pick your nation, maps (can be restricted to where what nation fought in) and how large the campaign and economy you start with is. There are research trees so expect to start with infantry heavily and work you way into armored cars then tanks etc.... missions play as a back and forth for rewards such as ammo and points to resupply and get new units. You research more units (unlock) with research points and spend them in your research tree. This lets you build your force to how you want to structure it. Want to be largely tanks? go for it. Want to focus on more elite infantry? go for it. Artillery? so on and so forth.

  TL:DR an in depth WW2 strategy game where you need to keep your troops and vehicles supplied and manage your units well, that also is great to play CO-OP with your friends, up to 8 players on campaigns. I recommend this game and will at some point write reviews on each DLC.

212274361.review:
Easily the best WW2 tactics game currently on the market.

Gameplay - very high learning curve, like high! But it's ultimately very rewarding. I mostly play on hard difficulty to see how far I can go on missions. Line of sight, flanking, logistics, air/artillery support - you name it, it's here. It really makes you feel like a mission commander with the level of immersion. 

Direct unit control works but it can be somewhat clunky. I like how the directly controlled unit does not magically transform into a hero unit - they are still confined by the rules of the game. When odds are stacked against you, you may find that taking direct unit control can sometimes turn the tide of battle. Had an epic encounter on the Finnish mission Stalin's Guns where I managed a flamethrower tank inside a village to take out unsuspecting T-34s by overheating them! Epic stuff and an equally tense moment.

Graphics - models are highly detailed, infantry movement on the battlefield is eerily reminiscent of WW2 combat footage on the Eastern Front. Effects are quite realistic.
Sound - units speak their own language so that's a plus plus in my books. Weapon sounds are booming. Rocket artillery launches are always a delight.

Not a perfect game by any means but really close. 8.9 / 10

Without a doubt, the best WWII RTS game I've ever played. The dev team continues to support through regular patches and DLC expansions, including new factions, units, maps, etc. Some DLCs definitely do more than others, but they all have strengths depending on what you're interested in.

Personally I mainly enjoy Conquest but Skirmish has a good variety of game modes, or you can play through scripted Campaign missions. I previously critiqued AI pathing but the devs have just introduced a feature that enables infantry to path and jump over vaultable objects automatically and is proving to make a stark difference in gameplay.

Ostfront has a strong modding community with an ever-expanding list of content including total conversion overhauls, and anyone can get into modding by using the dedicated editor tool included with the game if they wish.

I would strongly recommend this game to anyone who has a vested interest in the WWII era. The combination of RTS, the direct control of individual units and the freedom to manage their inventories, as well as dozens of other features and great visuals, is simply too good to miss out on.

211634589.review:
Let's not be afraid to say it – the best RTS of its kind on the market. In a certain sense, it's almost without competition if you're looking for realistic gameplay in the theater of World War II, since Sudden Strike 4 is just okay, Blitzkrieg 3 is bland as lukewarm tap water at its best moments, Company of Heroes 3 hasn't had much of an idea for itself since launch day, and Men of War II played a game against itself that it knows how to play and lost by mutual walkover, but that's another topic altogether.​

What you can love it for…

Unbelievable attention to detail – from uniforms, vehicles, weapon mechanics to the prepared maps.​

Absolutely extraordinary and unprecedented ability to perform epic actions on the battlefield. I don't know of another game of this type where you can select a single soldier who picks up a rocket launcher from a fallen enemy to flank an enemy tank from behind, hit it just right to set the ammo compartment on fire, leading to a turret-tossing spectacle where the turret crashes into a building, collapsing part of it and killing two enemy soldiers… nope, I just don't know of any.​

The complexity of everything we do: manage ammo, position units to the centimeter for optimal visibility, every battle is a challenge, every clash requires an individual approach, and sometimes you end up playing 5D chess with a well-placed and covered anti-tank gun if you don't have the right countermeasures.​

Co-op with another fan of the topic is a bullseye.​

…and what to think twice about

Uneven AI – unfortunately, both enemy and ally AI can be inconsistent, especially in conquest mode. They attack incoherently, defend clumsily, and sometimes feel like "spicy" shooting range dummies. It's not a total disaster and can surprise you at times, but it's an area where the developers still have work to do.​

Despite everything, a fairly high entry barrier, especially if you're not a fan of micromanagement.​

The full price with DLCs is a bit off-putting, but I can't say I regret the purchase (if someone wants to test if this type of game is for them, it's worth grabbing the original – Men of War: Assault Squad 2, which - on sale - costs less than a kebab).​

The rest is silence and depends on the player's preferences. No doubt it's a product aimed at a specific target audience, and if you're in it, you can sink many hours here.​

This game is an absolute masterpiece!

I play almost exclusively Dynamic Conquest, some of these features I mention don't apply as much in multiplayer.

You can micromanage inventories and take direct control of every individual unit on the field. Not only that, but they will be in every battle until they die or you dismiss them. Every person has a name. I actually care to keep everyone alive through every battle unlike other games where you just spawn more nameless pawns out of a barracks to send to the slaughter.

Tank warfare has been meticulously crafted. I never cared for tank battles in games until now. Armor is thicker/thinner at certain points, the size/type of munitions will play a major role in the outcome, and your tanks have actual crewmembers rather than it just being a lifeless hunk of metal. The tracks/engine can get damaged, leaving the tank stranded and vulnerable to molotovs, anti-tank grenades, etc. You'll have to make quick decisions such as choosing to evacuate your crew and have them run to safety while hoping they don't get mowed down by machine guns. 

Those are two of my favorite points but there is so much more.

There is still so much untapped potential in this game, and I hope they continue to work on this for years to come.

If you want a strategy game that was made with tremendous passion and attention to detail, this is it. I will happily pay extra for more DLCs and new games so long as the developers keep their spine and don't give in to the same ideologies that are showing up in the games of many AAA developers.

211343860.review:
It's an amazing game developed by devs that obviously love what they're doing. The AI is not the smartest, but the CPU AI is by design smarter than yours (or you'd just lean back and watch your AI do your work for you). Small annoyances here and there, but only detectable once you develop an obsession and put in hundreds of hours into the game ("why can I do this with [this vehicle] but not with [this other vehicle], type of annoyances). 

The Discord channel is great where you can report bugs (which are addressed in 99% of the cases, unless it's a bug introduced by the game engine, which may take longer to address), and suggest new features (but be prepared to make a case for why you want a specific unit/weapon/vehicle introduced, and oftentimes to other more knowledgeable community members with severe WW2 autism), etc. Modding is limited by the engine but there are amazing community modders out there whose mods have eventually made it into the core game. I wish they could work more on the Conquest Game mode a bit more, but the devs have made meaningful strides there as well. 

The game can trigger tons of emotions: anxiety, despair, victory-induced euphoria, adrenaline kicks, and pure satisfaction, and the occasional rage quitting.

I generally play Hell Let Loose, and I compensate the itch to have more overall macro control with micromanagement (and play other maps and environments) with Gates of Hell: Ostfront. Obviously not the same game, but they'll definitely scratch the same itch centers.

When played singleplayer this is an incredible real time strategy game, with a fantastic direct control mechanic and inventory system, an awesome sucessor to the men of war series.

However, when played in the multiplayer modes, whether it is the conquest campaign or the skirmish missions, it becomes both a comedy and an intense World War Two simulator. No other game I have played give you command of an entire platoon of troops, while letting you run around inside with a flamethrower, or give a MG-42 to your commanding officer taken from the hands of a deceased enemy soldier. The graphics may be aging compared to modern games, but in no way are bad, the lighting of a tank's machinegun on a night map is one of the greatest sights in video-games today.
This is the game you did not realise you wanted, but will love after you play it for the first time.

Call to Arms: Ostfront is exactly the evolution I always hoped to see from the classic Men of War series. As someone who has spent countless hours playing every MoW title, I can confidently say that Ostfront feels like a true step forward modernized, smarter, and more dynamic in every sense.

One of the standout improvements is the AI. Gone are the days of soldiers running into gunfire like they’re eager to meet the afterlife. Units behave with a level of intelligence that genuinely changes the flow of battle. They take cover intuitively, flank with purpose, and respond to threats with a situational awareness that makes every engagement feel intense and believable. Their use of support equipment and emplacements make them a lot more difficult to fight against and work around. It’s easily one of the biggest upgrades over Men of War and a major reason the game feels so fresh. Also the first person ability with direct controlling units while a bit gimmicky can be quite useful in some situations where line of sight is important and can be quite fun playing as a individual soldier.  

And then there are the dynamic campaigns, my absolute favourite addition. Each mission feels alive, with shifting objectives, changing battlefronts, and the sense that your decisions impact a larger campaign map. No two playthroughs feel the same. The way the game blends strategic planning with boots-on-the-ground direct control is just incredibly satisfying. I genuinely love diving into these campaigns; they keep me hooked for hours at a time.

Overall, Call to Arms: Ostfront is more than just a follow-up to Men of War, it’s an improvement in nearly every area. Better AI, deeper gameplay, more replayability, and a modern polish that breathes new life into the genre. I absolutely love what the developers have done here, and I can’t wait to sink even more time into its dynamic battlefields and for the new British faction update coming soon!
