157673203.review: This game is the best realistic tactical/strategic game. It is not like Company of Heroes, which is a pure rts game, where different units mostly have only differences in health/armor/attack/range/vision, etc. This game requires you to consider many scenarios in combat, such as micromanaging a grenadier to crawl forward to the side and rear of an enemy tank and throw a grenade. These detailed scenarios excellently restore the appearance of real war: when attacking, you need air strikes, artillery, and infantry coordination; when defending, you need to build fortifications on high ground, lay mines and anti-tank obstacles. At the same time, in many single-player missions, you are no longer required to just monotonously ‘eliminate the enemy’, many times you need to infiltrate behind enemy lines to obtain intelligence, provide cover for friendly convoy transfers, or even operate bombers to pinpoint and eliminate specific enemy targets… People say War Thunder restores history, but I think War Thunder compared to this game, can only be considered a driving simulator. Because real war is multi-branch coordination, happening in the air and on the ground at the same time. The mighty Tiger tank can indeed easily destroy the Soviet T34 series, but without engineers clearing mines, it can only step on mines and break down in front of the enemy line; without the cover of grenadiers, rushing into the enemy line can only become a target for anti-tank grenades and rocket launchers; without accompanying anti-aircraft fire, it will become a feast for the IL-2 attack aircraft… Just around one tank, there can be so many variables and choices, let alone the cooperation between different branches, terrain and tactics are completely diverse. Here, as a commander, you can command an armored column to push the enemy line; you can choose to concentrate artillery and air force to let the enemy experience the ‘Von Fritsch ammunition quantity’; you can also transform into a Brandenburg assault team, infiltrate behind the enemy, and attack from the enemy’s line depth in reverse. There is no simple armor-piercing confrontation in war, the most important thing is system operation. There is no such thing as a single superior weapon that can sweep the enemy in this world, only the cooperation between different branches can highlight the true appearance of war, and this is also the unique feature of this game.

157268394.review:
[h3] Summary and Rating [/h3]
[b]Preliminary note[/b]: 60 hours of playing time, standard campaign completed (easy), first Liberation DLC missions started

[b]Summary:[/b] Great realistic real-time strategy game with exciting and challenging missions, extensive optional micromanagement, base-building content, very wide variety in infantry, vehicles and air force and the ability to control each soldier/vehicle from a first-person perspective to get straight into the action.
[b]Buying recommendation:[/b] Yes (also at full price)
[b]Rating:[/b] 8/10 based on 
Gameplay: 9/10
Graphics: 7/10 
Sound, music and voices: 7/10 
Campaign: 9/10 
Technology: 8/10 
Extras: 9/10 (Editor + Modding)

[h3]Negative[/h3]
- no HUD scaling for higher resolutions (very annoying, should be introduced urgently)
- Revise training camp and make it more beginner-friendly / better define instructions
- sometimes missing designations for infantry

[h3]Performance / Bugs[/h3]
The game runs very well for me (32GB RAM, RTX 3060, Ryzen 7 5800X) on WQHD with ultra settings, the frames are stable, no major stutters. The game is largely bug-free, even if engineers sometimes install themselves and then can't move anymore (don't build tank barriers directly behind sandbags!). 

[h3]Campaign[/h3]
I really liked the missions in the standard game, even if the difficulty seems quite random and doesn't increase with each mission. This also depends on the different scenarios and the corresponding necessary knowledge about the game. Let's see how it works out in the second run on normal. I really like the design and content of the stories and intro videos. I also found the first missions of the Liberation DLC exciting, but I can't say anything final about them yet. Unfortunately, the training camp is very buggy and the instructions are sometimes completely unclear. At some point I gave up and started playing the real game. This is something that should be urgently improved for beginners, otherwise they will be put off before they really start playing. General tip: If a mission seems too difficult, you're probably using the wrong approach. Fundamentally rethink your tactics. Overall, the missions feel very dynamic, sometimes the main direction of battle changes or there are counterattacks after conquering the front or flanking opponents. In addition, there are small, fun secondary tasks that make the missions seem coherent. The only thing that sometimes bothers you is that the opponents unexpectedly come from directions that were not foreseen and defensive positions that have been built for 30 minutes are completely useless. But that's more exciting than annoying and doesn't happen all the time. Plus, it's probably realistic.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
The game is diverse and the mechanics seem well-rounded and realistic. 
I find it interesting that - like in other games - you can't always use the same tactics to win. It is absolutely necessary to play map-based and, for example, to use the landscape to your advantage. Heavy gun positions must be covered with smoke from the front in order to then flank them with infantry and tanks. Alternatively, you can take them out from a distance with your own heavy guns or let a hidden infantry unit flank you unnoticed in order to switch off the gun so that the tanks can advance can. The battlefield/road must be checked for mines or you risk losing entire groups of vehicles. If your own tank is disabled due to mistakes, you may have to take out enemy vehicles at close range with grenades, dynamite or explosives, which in turn often requires smokes or clever preemptive hiding of infantry units close to future front lines. Of course you can also use anti-tank infantry if available. In general, the variety of infantry units is very high and everything seems appropriate. Short-range assault troops can be equipped with SMGs, riflemen and flamethrowers to storm trenches. They receive cover fire from the riflemen/MGs from a greater distance. The lieutenant is used for reconnaissance with his binoculars, while snipers operate in the background. Medics then in the second infantry group, so that they don't die on the first attempt if there is a machine gun hidden somewhere by the fog - everything feels great dynamic, there are regular surprises that you have to be able to deal with. Basically, I often noticed that realistic tactics are effective in this game, which increases the immersion enormously: you can often act in a way that makes sense. There are epic wedge-shaped attacks on an area of ​​the front line, followed by flanking attacks and ambush attacks to take the entire front line. 

The switch between offensive and defensive also keeps longer battles exciting; in the latter, the base building elements in particular are a huge added value because you can determine your own tactical positions (hills, forests, intersections, roads), which are then filled with sandbags, trenches, holes, Barbed wire and anti-tank barriers can be secured. In addition to the previously distributed anti-tank mines and anti-personnel mines. You then have to reinforce these defensive positions with the right types of infantry / heavy weapons (mortars, anti-tank guns, artielly) / vehicles and thus have a lot of individual control over the battle and the map. Environmental features such as differences in altitude or poor visibility in forests are noticeably relevant. Micromanagement often becomes relevant later in the course of the battle: ammunition and supplies have to be replenished, this can be done at stationary points or in the vicinity of certain mobile vehicles. Here, too, you have great control over the structure of your front line, for example by moving or building ammunition depots of medical tents near a new front line. If you run out of ammunition, you can loot any enemy (weapons, ammunition, bandages, supplies, explosives) - so you can turn a simple rifleman into a machine gunman. After damage, every enemy vehicle can be looted and repaired so that you can then use it yourself. However, depending on the damage, this takes a very long time and is not possible if the vehicle has been completely destroyed. In this respect, you should use the opportunity to switch off special parts such as the tracks or the gun turret in order to render the vehicle unable to move or combat. Micromanagement is sometimes a bit awkward, but largely optional. This is rounded off by the innovative first-person option, which you can activate at any time for any soldier and get straight into the action. Simply take on the perspective of a soldier dynamically in the game: great! And in some situations, a life saver!

[h3]Dynamic campaign[/h3]

In addition to the campaign, there is also the dynamic campaign, which is preferred by many and offers the possibility of large and long turn-based battles.

[h3]Editor[/h3]

There is also an extensive editor with which you can create your own scenarios. Very extensive, for example it is possible to adjust individual life point values ​​per soldier. However, the editor is complex and I have only dealt with it superficially. Nevertheless, something like this is an absolute plus point for me in general because it means the game can be played endlessly and you don't necessarily have to buy DLCs. Always fair when developers make something like that possible. And for me a reason to buy DLCs at full price because I won't be forced to do it.

[h3]Modding[/h3]

There are mods, but I haven't tried them yet.

[h3]Music and voices[/h3]

Okay, not great, but suitable. The narrator in the intro videos does a very good job.

156536152.review:
It's Janky, but there are good bits. 6/10. I'd love to leave a positive review however more would need to be done. I support the devs however as i think they are going to turn this game into something really special.

Pro's

- Sound is amazing, from gun shots, that whipping sound of bullets as they pass units, explosions, the unit speech, engine sounds and pretty much all sound design and recordings are epic levels of good. Probably one of the best I've heard. 

- The graphics are decent, the effects, the maps themselves, it's great when it's paired with the sound effects as it really does simulate a real battlefield. 

- The game play is decent, there is a lot of mechanics at play, that feel rewarding when you get it right, though still janky.

- The Dynamic campaign and local AI skirmishes are the best modes.


Con's

- There is a LOT of jank, from clipping geometry ( invisible walls around terrain ) the way models interact with hit boxes particularly with the environment, you will notice this as your shots will hit invisible obstacles often, very pronounced in prone position or when your tank is hull down.

- The AI is rudimentary, from not responding, not shooting, Ai just running towards you, AI abuse vision mechanics the way a human can't. AI also get unlimited ammo, unlimited resources. Lazy way of making the game challenging. The developers know this is a challenge to code, because then they would need to write code of sending ammo to replenish it's units, which would be a massive job to code, so instead of actually doing that, they just give the AI unlimited everything, while you need to micromanage sending ammo boxes and supply trucks out to your units. 

- The moving path system mostly works okay, but units will often get stuck on geometry and obstacles in the environment and then just stop leaving you confused as to why they didn't move to where you asked them to.

- Bugs, where captured tanks won't move, but will rotate on same spot, units not responding to commands randomly.

- Basic things with the UI are tedious, for example if you want a crew to leave a vehicle you command them to exit, but then need to re-select the units to ask them to move, making you click a lot, the micro management is tedious rather than rewarding.

- The vision system is good in concept and works well for PVP, but for PVE or playing solo against AI, the AI abuses the mechanics and rather moves its units into places where you don't have vision. Basically, the AI checks where the player has no vision, then moves there, if you chase them down, they simply do it again, moving units specifically to where you can't see. It happens on a micro and macro scale which makes the fighting seem robotic and unnatural. After a few hundred hours you learn how to combat this silly behaviour but it's simply programmed that way in order to provide some artificial challenge.  To make it worse, AI on the player side does not do this, they never use smoke and don't abuse vision mechanics.

- The single player campaign missions are horrid, there is no open way to do things, you're told what to do in every single mission rather than giving the player the options on how they want to proceed. 

- All the good features like laying mines, building defences, sandbags, such a great idea, but the micro management you need to do by clicking and giving commands for everything renders it all useless because it takes you away from fighting for too long.

In the end, I'd say its a good game, I will thumbs it down because there is a lot that should be improved by default. 

There should also be more options to set up your own battles with your own settings, the custom settings in skirmish are so bareboned. It must allow us to set the parameters for every part of the battle, from which units are allowed, how many capture points.

The game has promising updates incomming, I will consider changing my review to positive if i deem the new features, content or efforts worth a thumbs up, the devs do seem like good people.

So it might actually be worth supporting them to make this product better.

Absolutely Fantastic! Realistic tactics, especially when it comes to tanks. Nothing beats the Tiger II, except maybe a direct hit from a 1000lb bomb or a player stupid enough to allow a flamethrower to get behind it and light the engine on fire. Some of the mods available on the workshop are must haves, like having Medics actually do their job without having to be told. 

Soviet play relies  heavily on infantry early on, but the second you can get a pair of T35s you'll be in good shape. T35s are mobile gun batteries and can handle any early tank or light vehicle head on, but beware anything above a 37mm will damage this thing quick and a 105 will blow this thing to hell and gone. Always keep bombers on standby as they are really the only thing you have that can deal with the later stage German tanks without getting instantly clapped. Heavy and clever usage of flame weapons is key and artillery is never a bad choice.

Germany is pretty heavy with the tanks. StuG III's will get you by for quite some time and the Flamethrower infantry can kill ANYTHING if they get the engine compartment alight. The second you can grab a Tiger II or perhaps a pair....its full on easy mode. Surviving long enough to get Tigers is another story.

US has an uphill battle at every turn. Your tanks are simply outclassed by Germany at every stage, I honestly still cannot believe how many 90mm shells a StuG III can weather and still kill the US counterpart with relative ease. The US excels at slapping infantry with tons of lead and even in the later stages of a campaign a Stuart is an invaluable friend to have. US tanks pack more punch than a lot of the German counterparts in the same stages but US tanks are made of paper while German tanks are solid rocks with guns attached. Even the Pershing gets slapped down by a Tiger II almost instantly, its for this reason Artillery is the US' best friend. Cumbersome to use, and VERY slow getting into position without a tow vehicle, but dish out the hurt from relative safety and at long range, oh and I never mentioned that later stage US tanks are actually howitzers on treads and unlike German counterparts can actually tow their own ammo supply. Jack of all trades and a master of none. As with the Soviets ALWAYS keep bombers in queue.

Finland is hard to play in conquest. With a mix of German and Soviet tech Finland's play style reflects an in-between those two. Infantry are essential throughout the entire campaign, as is AA, but with access to Panzer IV's the mid to late game is fairly good. Tanks with Finland are not the hardiest versions of any so clever positioning and reliance on flame weapons is a must. I have come to realize that AA is this factions best friend. Soviets bomb the ♥♥♥♥ out of you at almost every engagement after the first few so keep those Ford trucks around and aplenty, those Landswerk things are hot garbage. By far the best faction to go around in 3rd person mode with infantry, the Soviets always have plenty to mow down. I highly reccommend playing both Germany and Russia before tackling the Fins.

All in all a fantastic game that I will play for years.

[list]

[*]Talvisota brings Finland as a playable faction, introducing new vehicles, units, weapons, and missions.
[*]Liberation introduces the U.S. as a playable faction, adding Western Front content, including vehicles, units, weapons, and missions.
[/list]

As a conclusion, I really do recommend "Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront". On the other hand, if what you're seeking is a more casual experience similar to "Company of Heroes", then I'd suggest checking out "Men of War 2", releasing later this year.

156164350.review:
I always feel like I'm missing something when lots of people like a game but I don't so I worry I'm not being fair, but I can't recommend it as an average RTS player. I think this game has insane potential but it hurts my hand to play from just the sheer amount of micro required to do what the game is asking. There is some jankiness I'm happy to forgive for what I assume is a smaller studio, and it does some interesting things with the direct unit control that is really fun, as well as provide cool, satisfying battles and decent audio of crackling gunfire - explosions are the only let-down - but there is so much jank and weird design choices that it becomes near unplayable for me. Things always end up taking me way longer to do than they should because the instructions for anything are so vague that it feels like they weren't thoroughly playtested with other beginners. I often end up spending ages trying to understand what to do next. I want to like this, but it's pushing me away.

I think the most painful thing this game does (and why my hand hurts) is making you manage individual soldiers' or vehicles' inventories and ammo types in the most difficult way. This happens in lots of places: missions where you don't have resupply crates that do it for you when your units run out of ammo; or if you have to load ammo into a tank; or having to find a particular item in a field of dead soldiers (yes, you have to click through each body while holding the highlight bodies key); or if you want to look through vehicles that might have the supplies you need; or if a tank has to switch between firing at long and short range, or from hard targets to soft targets and its ammo type is suboptimal. Yeah, you do all that manually and it is not only painfully click-heavy, but also not a fun experience. 

The squad management is another bizarre design choice. I couldn't easily set up manual control groups, I had to select multiple units that will auto merge into a squad, but there are no hotkeys for these groups, just an emblem you can click to select them all. If I click an individual soldier, it will break them out of the squad and I have to reselect the rest to merge them as a squad again. Unless I completely botched it, it feels like in 2023 we're still reinventing the wheel of RTS controls and UI/UX. Given how finicky this all is, finding the soldier you need for a task in a big group is hilarious because everyone looks the same. The good version of this is if you have a group of soldiers with the items you need, their actions will be done automatically by the right person or object if you know what to click. The bad part is, sometimes doing things like mounting a machine gun is manual and you need to use the incredibly fiddly inventory system. To revive soldiers, you have to have a person with bandages selected somewhere in your units (not everyone has one), then manually click every soldier that goes down. Good luck finding the person with the medkits in their inventory across a mid size battlefield while managing the rest of your besieged units! Same goes for tank repair, there's about 5 clicks to repair a tank if you don't have the repair kit on your soldier so this gets old fast.

There are also no alerts when your men are being killed offscreen, so you just have to figure out how to keep track of it yourself. Again, this is a basic RTS feature strangely absent here. And as people have mentioned, missions don't end sometimes, or they do but if you click "continue" instead of "next", then you get left on the same map and have to manually quit and select the next mission yourself. I stopped playing after I spent about 45 minutes trying to figure out how to end the second Russian mission. Hilariously, there is a secret objective on that mission but it doesn't tell you what it is once you reveal it, the camera just zooms in on a part of the road with some crates, and when you fail, it zooms in on the road even further. After I had found the intel briefcase and picked it up, it never gave me further instruction. I have to presume it bugged and just didn't progress.

There is clearly a lot of love for the RTS in here, but I don't recommend this as it stands because it feels like they've gone with a lot of interesting features but not thought about user experience or playtested enough. I thought this might be more accessible than Men of War 2, which didn't give me a tutorial when I started. Though CTA does provide a tutorial, it still leaves the average person wondering how to enjoy most of what the designers envisioned.

Where do I begin - the extensive amount of units, atmosphere, level designs, campaigns, cooperative play? GoH: Ostfront has given me one of the most immersive WW2 RTS experiences (RTS genre - as a whole - as well) I've ever had. The campaign missions are extensive, and really make you feel like you are in some deep WW2 scenarios.

To those looking to dive into this game, this is not a competitive RTS. Factions are not balanced as such. This game is based more around realism, thus the campaigns and conquest mode shine the most, imo. I play multiplayer with my buddies sometimes, but you're not going to find automatch around here. Some may see it as a drawback; I more see it as a feature. This game is simply geared towards giving you the most immersive WW2 RTS experience out there.

Combat is very methodical and risky. Infantry go down quickly. Tanks can be knocked out in one shot depending on your opponent's strength of arms (there are penetration values based on armaments being used). There are tanks that simply cannot be penetrated based on armor, but you could knock out a track.

I could go on. If this game sounds like it's up your alley, buy it!

155583922.review:
What is this game?
Basically Men of War. If you don't know what that means: you spawn units (infantry, tanks, support equipment) and control them. No base building & resources gathering.

What does it add compared to Men of War?
- Newer graphics
- Third person mode & first person mode (some vehicles)

What's single player like?
Note: I only played single player a little as it quickly felt repetitive and not fun.
You have several campaigns and a 'conquest' mode. They all come down to the same gameplay.
You kill the helpless enemies using artillery, tanks and well placed mines while minimising losses.
The challenge is fighting off wave after wave or assaulting a superior foe with limited resources.

What's multiplayer like?
Starting off the lobby system is broken and you will struggle to host or connect with lobbies regardless of your isp, region or pc. Say 1 out of 3 matches end quickly because someone fails loading or lags unbearably. Once in a match you can spawn units based on timers (look up men of war). Infantry, armoured cars and support guns are unlocked first, later tanks and heavy artillery at the end. Often a match snowballs hard and you won't even get to unlock your late game units.

MP game modes:
- conquest (coop vs ai dynamic campaign)
- coop (coop vs ai missions)
- battle zones (classical victory points mode)
- domination

There is no attack/defence mode unlike men of war (one of the reasons you're better off buying that).

Battle zones is straight forward, rush to capture points and hold them until your team reaches the required points. Losing units reduces your victory points. If you reach 0, you lose (depending on a setting). If you fail to rush the capture points, you have to attack and capture more. Sometimes this mode snowballs heavily but often the matches are somewhat interesting as there are many (> 5 typically) capture zones spread around the map. This mode tends to end quickly if the team that lost early on doesn't make a big comeback mid game.

Domination is in my opinion the best mode. Each team has a HQ sector, lose it and you lose the match. New capture zones are spawned every now and then in a semi-predictable pattern. Capturing these zones gives you extra manpower & victory points. This tends to move the battle around the map to some degree, which is good. The placement of the sectors can be very one sided. If the first few sectors spawn in territory you already control, you get extra manpower & victory points basically for free. This causes snowballing.

Performance:
Straight up terrible. No point lying here. The game looks good compared to men of war but it requires 7-17GB of ram runtime. Whenever 1 person lags in a match, the entire game becomes a slide show. I'm not sure if the devs simply didn't optimise it or if the engine is crap but the result is clearly terrible. Also players frequently suffer from lag spikes of whole seconds despite their internet working fine. I believe that is an issue with the game itself. An issue I did not experience in Men of War.

The balance:
The balance between factions and doctrines has shifted drastically several times. I think that overall it's not bad. It's neither Wehraboo heaven nor Soviet propaganda movie. Sadly the game suffers heavily from pay to win DLCs. Most DLCs add a new faction & new doctrines to the old faction (alongside maps & missions). To get people to buy the DLC, the new faction & doctrines are intentionally made more powerful than the existing factions & doctrines. This is called powercreep. By the time the next DLC comes out, the devs will/have nerfed the previous DLC to be about balanced.

So what about the gameplay itself?
You can order your units to move, fire, attack, etc, let them fire at will or directly control them. The difference between these is sadly massive. The units AI retarded (more on that below). This means that direct control or constant ordering is the only viable way to play. You don't have the resources (unless you play custom/test mode) to trust the unit AI.

Infantry combat boils down to grenades + (s)MGs + snipers (+ support guns). Tank combat supposedly is deterministic and realistic, but ends up pretty random as hit chance is random. If you aim the right spots with the right gun, tank combat is 1 hit kill. Note you can only hit these weakspots (somewhat) reliably if you use direct control.

As you are constantly required to micro units, you tend to play with 2 dozen infantrymen 1-2 tanks and some support guns. This hurts the setting of ww2, the largest scale war ever...
Also the micro makes the game stressful instead relaxing. And so it fails to be a proper game, it's more of a chore.

What's so bad about the unit AI?
- Infantry will lie down and cower behind cover and not fire. You can workaround this by putting them in the open and ordering them to lie down. If you like using cover to gain tactical advantage, I sadly have to recommend Company of Heroes over this.
- Vehicle path finding is terrible. Vehicles prefer to drive over roads (makes sense) except the roads almost always go through the center of the map where the enemy can easily hit you. To work around this you have to double right click (be sure to check the path preview) or manually drive (let's you go faster also).
- Units love to pick their own targets, often preferring to kill a harmless infantrymen vs an enemy tank or support gun.
- Infantry turns to face the direction of combat. Makes sense, you may think. Except they never turn back to face the way you want them to face. This makes keeping vision on an area micro intensive as you have to tell every infantrymen personally to face a certain direction. He will look away the moment he senses combat somewhere.
- Vehicles love turning on the spot instead of driving in an arc. This makes them slow and exposes their weak spots.
- Infantry does not use grenades or AT rockets automatically most of the time. Very rarely they do. It's so rare, you can't rely on it.

Other issues:
- Infrequent crashes to desktop.
- Poor map design with a lot of tiny height differences that are hard to spot. You can find them if you go first person mode or tilt your camera to the ground.
- Units have dementia and forget where the enemy is despite aiming at it. This is not so much an issue with artillery duels but mostly with tank combat.
- There are bombing runs you can call in but they are laughably easy to dodge by just stepping aside or towing a gun and driving away. Only useful vs vehicles with broken tracks or the karl gerat.

Summary:
Buy Men of War (any version) if you like to micro. It's cheaper and you won't miss anything.
If you want better unit AI and cover to matter, buy Company of Heroes (+ mods).

Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront suffers from excessive focus on micro, snowballing, pay to win, old engine, terrible unit AI, terrible networking code and performance issues.

The best advice for the devs is just build a new engine and fundamentally fix issues or just make Men of War mods.

AI:

	This game has some of the worst AI that I have ever seen in a video game. The soldiers in this game are the most inept bunch of unresponsive losers that you can imagine. Often they don't even want to shoot at each other, its the strangest thing ever, the guy with a rocket-launcher is right in front of him but he doesn't even acknowledge that something is off or even on which planet he is currently on. When the AI finally decides to wake up, their choice of target is often backwards, for example an MG will decide to shoot at random infantry instead of the AT gun slightly behind them. A gun whose exposed operators can easily be gunned down by a dozen rounds. Another example is when an half-track with a completely exposed gunner drives up to your infantry squad, the infantry ᛋhit themselves and just stand there awkwardly while getting absolutely ᚠucked up by the main gunner who could be shot at any time. YOU have to click on the soldier, click the direct control button and aim at the gunner to kill him. If you tell your soldiers to target him, they will pull out grenades and rush at him. As a matter of fact, YOU have to directly control the entire front line to keep them shooting right, YOU have to be everywhere at the same time because if you are not, the AI will ignore the AT guns and Tanks and instead shoot at infantry hiding in trenches. Your tanks and vehicles will also choose to use valuable HE rounds at meaningless one man targets, which is why they quickly run out ammo. And on top of everything, this is happening all at the same time... My new favorite method of playing is to completely ditch these moᚱons and just grab a Sniper, give him AT weapons and snipe everyone in direct control mode. By the end of the mission, he has hundreds of kills and dozens of tank kills. Overall the AI and targeting mechanics are very very frustrating.

Single-player Campaign:

	The Campaign missions are varied in quality and interesting content, some I gladly replay while others I avoid entirely. I mostly play the German and Finnish missions. First of all, I want to say that most of the time I don't really feel like I am at war, it feels like I am participating in small border skirmishes, 100 men, sometimes even less, against a couple hundred soviets at most. The trenches are mostly empty, with only 5 guys sitting in one, you have a handful of AT guns and a couple tanks and armored vehicles. The campaign also lacks important battles, instead of fighting in a downtown soviet city, you will be fighting in a small village nobody has ever heard of or literally in the middle of nowhere Russia. This to me is huge wasted potential, not only are the missions so few in number, they lack any interesting location. One mission was leading a group of gebirgsjäger to some mountain station where you have to assassinate guards. 
	The closest thing you have to downtown battles are the ones found in skirmish, but they are only in a small part of the city. In Stalingrad, you fight over the Mamayev Kurgan, not in the actual city, instead, the battle for the city is reserved for the Soviets. There is also a Berlin defense mission for the Germans, but most of the map is the park area infront of the Reichstag, the rest is a couple of streets with ruined buildings. The skirmish missions themselves are not very many, 4 for each faction. They are ok at first but get more and more frustrating when you start getting past invisible triggers on the map where the further you go, the more high tier units they start endlessly spawning. And these waves never stop, they are set to be infinite, not only that but the cooldowns between their spawns decrease more and more to the point where its constant attacks. I personally really don't like this infinite enemy spawn choice, this is a very old and outdated thing, I remember getting angry in the old Call of Duty games because the enemies never stop popping out of nowhere. This design is older than the T-Rex, I think it would have been better if they had a limited amount of waves, it still could be a really high number of them but having them be infinite frustrates the player and makes it unfair because he has to spend a lot of points calling in reinforcements, meanwhile the AI gets to respawn every 10 seconds. But at the end I would consider the main campaign the best part of the game, mostly because its chill, and I can play as a sniper who kills everyone. 

Conquest:

	Conquest mode is extremely difficult for me to play, borderline impossible, especially if you have mods. It used to crash for me every time I tried to play it, then I managed to get it to work by changing some settings, but when you click start for a mission, you take a very long time to load, with mods, that load time can be up to 40 minutes of waiting. And when you finally load the mission, (if you don't crash) the game will give your days of playing Skyrim on a laptop a run for their money. The stuttering is constant, you can not even look around the map without stuttering, even when you pause the game to give the game a rest. This can last up to 10-15 minutes of mission time, after that it calms down significantly. The conquest missions themselves are also very frustrating and limiting to the player. You only have a couple squads or tanks under your control, again, this feels very small in scale compared to real battles. Its called "Conquest" but feels more like another skirmish battle. Also conquest is where all the bad parts of the game collide with everything else, there is no saving or slowing down, you HAVE to do your best at all times or you could easily lose a battle because the enemy loves spamming tanks, AT guns, Artillery, and infantry with bazookas, as well as deadly rifle grenades which can easily pass unnoticed until its too late. Combined with the lack of many friendly units, its easy to get overwhelmed unless the map is quite favorable to you and you play on low difficulty. And if you don't play with Fog of War off, God can only save you, because the enemy artillery is a pain. Although an interesting concept, conquest falls flat. 

MP Skirmish:

	Multiplayer Skirmish against the AI is alright, it can be fun, especially the bigger battles where you can have a full team and feel like you are really fighting in a real war. If you are playing by yourself, it can be frustrating, usually because the units themselves don't know how to shoot, you have to be controlling them. Skirmish with players is also pretty solid and interesting.

Workshop Mods:

	The workshop mods are quite excellent, everything from realism mods to missions, to skins, its very cool and extensive, and it has kept me interested in the game. I use mods that add accuracy to your gun while in direct control and also increase damage. Another one is where it allows you to aim down iron sights of most guns in the game, which makes everything a million times better for me and makes me feel immersed. Playing as a schizophrenic sniper is alot better.

Closing:

	What I would like to see is conquest being fixed, new modes, a better AI, path finding, more and more quality changes, an official addition of first person mode where you can play it like a Red Orchestra game. Censored swastika flags made me cringe, the germans are hoisting flags of a country that doesn't exist. The Finnish swastikas are also removed, which is much more strange to me since they were using it for a very long time, and they were not a National Socialist state. Overall, despite all the things that bother me about this game, I want to like it and I enjoy playing it my way, but I don't think I could recommend it in its current state, especially after the technical issues with the Liberation DLC. I don't really care about adding more factions to the game, I don't find the British, Italians, Japanese, or Polish interesting to me. Maybe it would be cool if they added the Hungarians or put in more foreign volunteers into the German army.

It's COH for grown ups. 

I'm a fan of games like COH and Warno but both got boring. So I got this in the christmas sale after ignoring it for years thinking it was just a modded version of MOW:AS2, which I didn't particularly like. I was completely wrong and I regret not getting it earlier. In terms of complexity and realism this just blows games like COH out of the water.

In contrast with simpler RTS games, where winning boils down to just out-microing your opponent, this game expects you to think logically and follow a plan. For example, in a recent PVP I encountered an enemy-held point occupied by a bunch of infantry in trenches. I used my COH brain, and ran at him with a mass of infantry and a couple of supporting vehicles, which in most other games would probably work. It was a disaster and the whole force was mowed down in under 30 seconds. This game is very punishing of 'brute force' tactics like that.
However, if I'd leopard-crawled a scout close to the position, used an artillery observer's flare gun to call artillery on him, and then sprinted an SMG squad covered by a bunch of smoke grenades to mop up the survivors, I could've taken the whole position without losing a single man. Point is, you have to think smarter, not just faster, than your opponent and that sets this apart from every other RTS I've played lately.
 
Fully reccomend this if you're bored to death of 'dumb' clicky and gimmicky RTS games that rely on exploits and map knowledge and APM.

154051425.review:
GoH Ostfront is advertised as a "realistic RTS game that offers endless replay value" and provides some "serious immersion" to the player. Let's dissect this a little: 
 
[b] Realism [/b] 
Infantry has visible health bars above their heads and can take several hits before getting killed, tanks and guns have a maximum shooting range of 100-200 meters (!) and even artillery cannot reach much further. Planes fly so low and slow that it's almost cartoonish and 20mm AA guns have better armor penetration values across the board than 3,7cm AT guns. So much for that.
 
[b] Replayability [/b]
The game offers several campaigns, individual skirmish battles and dynamic campaigns which are basically a series of skirmishes where you keep your troops. Normal campaign missions are embedded into a historical setting which definitely adds some flavor, however the mission design is rather simple and mainly consists of attack missions where you dig through a multi-layered frontline or defense missions where your troops are already in position upon mission start so you don't have to do much. The campaigns are ok during the first playthrough but have little replay value. Dynamic campaigns sound interesting on paper but are neither very dynamic nor especially interesting. You start with a generic 2D map which has your own HQ on the left and the enemy HQ on the right, both are connected through several missions from which you can choose your next battle. These are always alternating attack and defense missions where you either rush to conquer zones A+B or rush to occupy zones A+B and defend them afterwards. The only interesting part here is to see your new units in action which you have researched between battles, apart from that the missions are so monotonous and predictable that they get old quite fast.
 
[b] Immersion [/b] 
On a larger scale you can find some immersion in the normal campaigns due to their historic setting, but the dynamic campaigns are so artificial and basic that I find it impossible to get immersed in the slightest. There are no years, no seasons, no strategic points on the map and no tactical elements. It's really just a number of random skirmish battles without a logical connection to each other. You can't even tell if you are early or late in the war, since the enemies you encounter solely depend on what you send to the battlefield: In one mission you can send Pz IV and will face T-34 + KV1 suggesting that you are in mid-late war, but if you replace the Pz IV with Pz 35(t) in the next mission you will run into early war light tanks again as if you jumped back in time. If you look for the opposite of immersion in a WW2 game, this is it. And not only does the quality of the enemy forces scale with your own, the quantity does as well. So in the end there is little incentive to build a stronger and larger combat group since the enemy will just scale up his own forces in the same way.
 
[b] QoL and overall playability [/b] 
Both the AI and pathfinding are atrocious in this game. Ordering Infantry squads to walk left and right of the road so that tanks can pass through in the middle will frequently result in a blob of units that obstruct each other’s movement. Tanks have a tendency to present their lightly armored rear to the enemy and simply ignore when being fired upon. After digging foxholes, Infantry prefers to stand right next to them on open ground - even under fire. Even though you need to micromanage and babysit every single unit, it is not possible to give commands when the game is paused which can be immensely frustrating. A lot of unit functions can only be accessed through a small menu which is a heritage from previous games and absolutely outdated nowadays. In the unit research screen you cannot preview units before unlocking them, and in case they have lengthy names which do not fit into the textboxes you cannot even understand which unit you are about to unlock. Sorting your troops in the unit roster is not possible, saving unit setups for different missions is not possible and the list goes on.
 
[b] Conclusion [/b] 
Despite the many negative aspects the game can be fun to play, especially if you do the missions in coop with a friend. However, even years after release it still feels like an early access title which needs a lot more work. The Devs do regularly post development updates but I cannot see that the game is progressing at all and the many basic issues will apparently never be addressed. Instead, the focus is clearly on the production of more DLCs to further milk the community without fixing the base game. Therefore I cannot recommend GoH Ostfront, it might be ok for more casual players if picked up on sale, for those who want a more serious approach to WW2 RTS the Steel Division series is a much better choice.

- Extreme clunkiness ruins the game.

- My overall gripe is the amount of micro-management. 
- The micro would be fine IF you could issue orders while the game is paused. But you can't which sucks so hard.
- Given that you can't issue orders while paused, it is so annoying that units are dumb as ♥♥♥♥. "Hey guys. Look at that nice trench right beside us! Let's stand beside it instead" ... Order unit into trench ... "I'll just run through withering fire instead of choosing the safe route".
- the UI is incredibly clunky. Why do I need to press three times (with my mouse even) to do anything. 
- The person who made the keyboard shortcut layout should be fired. It can be kinda fixed yourself, but it is so illogically built.
- There is a cool "Build sandbags in front of my gun button". So you press it of course. Now your gun can't really turn anymore because some of the sandbags on the right and left are slighty too tall for the gun to shoot over. So very clunky.

The micro would be fine, as I said, if units did more themselves. 

- Why is there no "Gather supplies button"? No, instead you have to pick the INDIVIDUAL soldier you want to resupply, click each and every single thing you want to resupply from, and individually move every item. Resupplying a small unit of 10 soldiers can literally take 15 minutes. I kid you not.
- Why is there no "vision button" so we can tell if units can see/cover an area? It is incredibly hard to place units correctly.
- Buildings are so annoying too. You have to micro each soldier to each window. Like come on. Why is there no "Occupy building button" and then I click drag in the direction I want covered. Oh no. Even when you can (kind of) press "Occupy" the units occupy the build like they're idiots.

Another gripe is the lack of info in the game. It seems that the devolopers need somebody who isn't an engineer to do their UI. For instance the research screen in conquest gives NO INFO on what the thing you research actually does. Instead of a simple mouse-over popup that says "This unlocks this vehicle which has this gun and is good for this" you have to close the research-screen, then scroll through the 70-100 different units to find what you want to research. "Oh that wasn't what I wanted". Repeat this process for 15 minutes after every level untill you finally become an expert on German military unit-naming. Again clunkiness hinders the game-experience.

Every unit is so important and a slight mistake (because of the clunkiness mentioned above) can cost you a whole unit. So the micro kills the game for me. It is so so so very clunky. You pause constantly or you lose units because they can't think for themselves.

The game has potential, but if you actually want to call it an RTS, then look at good RTS's like Starcraft 2's interface which is incredibly intuitive and the hotkey setup is transferable (in muscle memory" from unit to unit.

This was kind of a rant, but I honestly think a justifiable one. This is not an RTS. It is a clunky micro-mess.

Hands down the best WW2 RTS to date. After 600 hours I still find myself playing it daily. This game is so good that it ruined my ability to play other WW2 RTS games like COH3. It makes the other games look like a cheap knock off. I should mention I have only played the campaign and conquest. The new expansion is also well worth its price with tons of new content and a new faction.

The good:

Unlimited replay-ability for conquest. 

You can customize your battle group to your liking. A CP point system is used for each call in, this prevents just rolling in with 20 tiger tanks. Even with this you can bring so many different types of units to the field.

Top notch graphics and effects

Challenging AI. Over the years the AI has gotten much better. I find myself surprised sometimes with a flanking maneuver that wipes out my artillery way behind the lines. The AI can and will wreck you at higher difficulties. 

This game forces you to use strategy and not just spam rush for objectives. With the pacing you face in conquest most battles will take 30-60 minutes. You need to plan out attacks and micro your units to make sure they dont get wiped out.

The bad:

Weird pathing issues that can happen. For example a tank will run over your friendly machine gun or randomly flip over and destroy the tank. I have seen trucks back into an artillery piece and blow both up. This is very frustrating when you cant afford those loses and you stuff dies to something dumb like this.

CP point system. While it has its advantages, I wish the base game expanded it out a bit. I am currently using a MOD which doubles the CP points in conquest which makes things last longer and gives the ability to bring in more units. They recently raised the cost on tanks which really limits how many can come into battle. This can be really challenging since the AI can spam more units then you. I hope they add the ability to customize the CP points for conquest in the base game.

High learning curve. This game is very unforgiving when you make mistakes. Spend an hour unlocking expensive heavy tanks, pay high CP to bring it into battle, 5 minutes later a random flamethrower destroys it. Or not bringing in artillery and the AI starts to destroy your units at range. I highly recommend looking at YouTube videos that cover the basics. Once you learn it, the game is extremely rewarding and fun.   

Long battles. This game in conquest will take on average 30-60 minutes per battle. This is not a game you sit down to play casually for a few minutes. I have even had a few run beyond that point. This happens more often with offensive battles. 


Overall I cannot say enough about how great this game is. The devs do a solid job releasing content and fixes for bugs. I would give it a 15/10 and highly recommend you pick this game up and check it out. Be warned that once you play and get into it, the bar is set REALLY high for other games and you will find yourself returning back here instead of the new game you just bought for your RTS fix.

An RTS has to be challenging, I went through a Conquest on Hardcore with 30W-0L, you really have to lose on purpose there's no way a player could lose against the AI on defence or attack unless you've never ever played a strategy game before.

The enemy AI literally tries to attack a tank up front with riflemen (not even kidding), they don't flank, they don't change strategy, the developers couldn't develop a good enough AI so they decided to send 200 men against your 50 men and thinking it's "more" difficult, it's a slaughterhouse nothing more nothing less, the difficulty is superficial, hardcore or easy doesn't make the AI better, the game simply sends more dumb troops on the same path to get shredded especially when you defend, then at some point they'll come with 20 tanks when you barely have enough CP to buy 3 tanks.

I wish the AI was smarter and more challenging because the gameplay is really good, the freedom of actions, interactions of your troops is very immersive, but unfortunately when there's zero challenge there's no fun unless you want a slaughterhouse.

I was recommended the mod called "Conquest Enhanced", it doesn't enhanced anything, all it does is give the AI better units in even larger numbers.

152535340.review:
Gates of Hell is the WW2 RTS game I always wanted. 

I thought I'd offer a non-exhaustive list of cool features for anyone thinking about buying this game;

-the maps are recreations of actual battlefields from the war using elevation data and recon photos n' stuff. 
-the buildings/environment can be destroyed 
-fires can spread 
-infantry can hitch a ride on your tanks
-3rd person control available for each individual unit
-you can micromanage each soldier/vehicle's inventory, (if you want)
-multiple game modes both on and offline
-co-op with or against your friends

It is a very challenging game, but that's part of the fun! If you try to rush in you'll most likely get slaughtered. To be successful in PVE you'll need to be cautious, lay down a base of fire with your MG's and artillery before pushing your infantry and armor towards an objective.

After logging over 700 hrs in this game I can highly recommend it to anyone who is a WW2 or RTS enthusiast.

Edit:
I have now surpassed 1000 hrs in-game at this point and I'm enjoying the Finest Hour DLC very much! 
There were a few bugs at launch, but those have been patched out the day after release. 

This dev team continues to impress with amazingly detailed models of our favorite machines that have detailed damage models and ballistic vs armor calculations that make armored combat more interesting and intense than any other RTS I've ever played.

Playing Gates of Hell brings me back to my childhood memories of playing with plastic models of Sherman & Churchill tanks vs Tigers & Panzer IV's in the dirt, digging trenches for my plastic army men and having them do battle, but so much more in depth and technical. I love it!

Firstly, I'd like to highlight that Gates of Hell: Ostfront is not just a DLC; it's a complete replacement for the base game, Call to Arms.
As someone who believes that video game prices have been on the rise and many publishers are not investing enough in promoting innovative gameplay, I must commend Barbedwire Studios and Digitalmindsoft for their exceptional work on this DLC.

In my extensive history of playing video games since my introduction to my father's PlayStation system in 1998, this is the first time I've been genuinely surprised, pleased, and excited by a company delivering a DLC that surpasses the quality of its base game.


While my only disappointment lies in the fact that you need the base game to play this DLC, I am delighted to express my love for Gates of Hell: Ostfront. It stands out as a shining example of what developers and publishers can achieve when they put effort into creating a substantial and well-crafted expansion. In an industry where companies often overprice or release half-baked products with microtransactions as a measure of success, this DLC has been meticulously built and beautifully executed.

I can't help but imagine the potential of a sequel, possibly on a powerful engine like Unreal Engine 5, or even a proprietary engine developed by the studio.

I wholeheartedly give this remarkable game's DLC a perfect rating of 5 out of 5 or 10 out of 10 for those purists out there.

I strongly recommend this game to anyone who may have had reservations about the base game. Gates of Hell: Ostfront serves as a masterclass for developers and publishers on how to create a substantial and enjoyable DLC for a game.

The Clunky UI inherited from Assault Squad is improved, and some of the OCD detail about which pocket you put your paper clips in and so forth also gone.

150388831.review:
I somewhat enjoy this game most of the time, but it is full of problems that make me not recommend it.

 First of all, and most importantly: Optimization.
 The game runs like complete ass most of the time; it stutters like hell, even when your FPS is good, the game just feels slow and everything looks kinda stuttery and off. It takes a ridiculous amount of time to load into anything if you have it installed on an HDD (like 5-10 minutes sometimes, even on simple missions). It also uses up ridiculous amounts of RAM because for some reason, the devs thought it was a good idea to cache into the RAM literally every single unit a faction has, regardless of it being used or not. I have 16gb of RAM, which is enough for most decently optimized games from my experience (and this is not one of them). When playing with only 2 factions, my PC will sometimes run out of RAM before the game even finishes loading into a match. When it comes to the conquest gamemode, i have no idea why, but it's even worse.

The game doesn't even look that good either. If you have a supercomputer and can play with maximum graphics somehow, it does look pretty good, but if you set the graphics to lowest, it will look like an exceptionally ugly ps2 game and still run like absolute ♥♥♥♥.

Second issue I have: Feedback.
From my experience, the devs don't even seem to look into the feedback section of their discord unless it's some very active member that posted it. The few moderators I've had the displeasure of interacting with were complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ too. I once posted a feedback thread on a certain gameplay issue, and I had my post deleted by a moderator because "there is already a similar post". Said similar post was from literally years ago and was buried so deep in the threads, no one was likely ever gonna find it. 

Any performance complaint you make is responded by a thousand NPCs saying the classic "just buy a new pc". 

The community is also a problem: They are mostly completely uncritical of the game or the devs behind it. Every single update post on steam is flooded with comments just praising the devs. The game is still full of fundamental issues but all I ever see is people praising the devs for correcting some fairly unimportant bugs.

Third issue: Content updates.
I have probably noticed how the game's title on steam explicitly says this is an EASTERT FRONT GAME (Ostfront), yet the devs have been neglecting the Soviet and Finnish factions for a very long time. First of all: the Germans have a much greater variety of units than the soviets have. The Finnish have very little variety, are not really fun to play as, and people only play them as a meme. Some years ago i think, they introduced the US Army faction to this explicitly specified EASTERN FRONT GAME. The american infantry units had much better graphical fidelity than the other infantry units present in the game, so they improved the quality of the German units shortly after. And then, the devs apparently spent an entire year developing a SECOND United States DLC in the meantime (completely unasked for), and only then, I guess they decided they should finally improve the Soviet infantry units. They've also forgotten to improve a few of the soviet infantry units and still haven't updated the Finnish ones. They still look like ps1 models, and now they're also working on adding a new western front DLC to an EASTERN FRONT GAME.

And the worst part of this is that all of these content updates seem to come in the form of overpriced DLCs. It has become very evident for me that these devs are only interested in milking money from western players who aparently, will only play their game if they can play as the most overrated and overrepresented faction in WW2 games: the US armed forces.

4th issue: Gameplay and Content Quality.
The game is clunky as hell, it feels unresponsive, unintuitive, and is bloated with useless mechanics. The AI is also complete garbage, and will completely ♥♥♥♥ up engagements they should be easily winning. Some orders work for certain units but do not work for others, even though they are available for both. Units will often prioritize targeting enemies that are out of sight, will randomly aim at enemies through terrain instead of targeting the ones they can actually engage. Vehicles and emplacements are extremely wasteful. Instead of firing in accurate bursts, they will completely unload their ammo at an infantryman 200m away and miss 90% of their shots because the game has an accuracy bloom system, but the AI clearly does not account for it.

The unit pathfinding is atrocious. Units will take terrible paths to the place you told them to go to. Emplacements will frequently get stuck on terrain, tanks will drive into unecessary obstacles that complelely slow them down instead of going around them, and when they do actually go around them, the will move, stop to make a turn, and then turn on their axis instead of making a long gradual turn that would have been much faster. Moving vehicles will often completely stop when you give them a new move order while they are moving.

The direct control mechanic is a liability instead of being just a cool gimick. The AI is so bad you'll frequently have to intervene with direct control to do their job for them. The direct control also feels slow and laggy, even on single player, and it's not fun to use.

The game also lacks the essential "reverse" order for vehicles, meaning you can't reliably tell them to reverse.

Wheeled SPGs with no turret need to be babysitted constantly because they cannot move on their own when the enemy is outside of their line of sight. Setting them to a certain position is also very annoying without direct controlling them.

The multiplayer experience is also really bad. Most people only play on private lobbies, or for some reason will leave the lobby as public and imediately kick you when you join. When you do get into a lobby though, the actual gaming experience is usually awful because of the terrible optimization this game has. So anyone in the lobby starts struggling with their PC or internet, the server will slowdown and often freeze up until the player stabilizes again.

5th Issue: Campaign missions.
I have only played the soviet campaign, so I can't speak for the other nations, but the soviet campaign completely sucks. Few missions in there are actually fun, but most of them give you so little units with no possibility of reinforcements, that they all end up turning into stealth missions. They will give you a single partisan squad and tell you to siege a german HQ, they will give you 4 spetsnaz guys and tell you to sabotage a huge german backline full of tanks and infantry (this one mission is kinda cool though, but most missions i played end up being like that). You don't ever get to engage the enemy as an opposing army, istead all of them feel like a bad call of duty campaign with characters that easily die and can't be replaced or reinforced.

There's probably more things to complain about but I'm already tired of writing this. Have a good day.

150087832.review:
[b]Gates of Hell is a game thats a lot like being in an abusive relationship, at one side you absolutely love the look and feel, but at the other hand once you get to know its mostly just painful.[/b]

[h3]Positive[/h3]
So let me just start off on the positive note here, 

[b]Atmosphere[/b]
the game itself is frankly beautiful, all the DLC's maps are extremely well made and very atmospheric with plenty of detail, the lightning in some maps is astonishing specially the winter maps, winter actually feels like winter, as someone born in the Arctic, its nostalgic and you can almost feel the cold damp wind on some maps.

[b]Models[/b]
The game models are likewise, very well researched, extremely diverse and well detailed, for a strategy game its almost hard to understand how well the models are and they keep improving them and adding even more details which can be a detriment, more on that later.

[b]Sounds[/b]
Often under looked in games, films and TV shows, but sound is arguably the most important aspect of them all, sound is the most immersive factor its what made games like STALKER and Half Life 2 so memorable, it was the sounds. 

Gates of Hell is no exception, the sounds are exceptionally good, every gunshot feels impressive, very close to real life without your ears bleeding afterwards, a cannon firing even a 50mm sounds quite powerful as it should, a big field howitzer will deafen the entire battlefield and explosions are just as impressive with ricochet properly sounded, you can even hear artillery shells as they come down on you.

[h3]Negative[/h3]
While that sounds fine and all, there is just way too much in the negative aspect to cover.

[b]Performance[/b]
This game is poorly optimised, and a huge detriment to that may just be the game engine which dates back to 2005, and the excessive amount of details everything have, for a RTS game, its quite frankly unnecessary for tanks to have their insides modelled, impressive yes but from a gameplay aspect you almost never zoom in enough nor often enough to admire these features, to my understanding the developers are quite proud of this excessive details in the game. 
Very few times have I heard anyone talk about the quality models however, because people are more interested in playing the game than to look at the models. The models however remain impressive to look at, but its unnecessary feature that ends up bogging the game down hard.

[b]The AI[/b]
This is arguably the most important aspect for ANY RTS games, in GoH its a HUGE drawback, frankly its hard to recommend this game at all if you have any form of self-respect to your own time. 
The AI which you fight against, is literally braindead, its so basic and so void of any strategical thinking its laughable, there games from the late 1990s that had more complex combat AI then this, Empire Earth for example had AI that would strategize best methods for attack, there no such thing in GoH.

Whats more obnoxious is your OWN infantry AI or tank AI are broken, the infantry AI in general can only target one enemy at a time, no I mean it, one enemy SOLDIER or TANK at a time, thats right, they are incapable of multiple target selection, such basic code is unavailable.
Another issue thats neck breaking is that tanks or any vehicle have weird target parameters, they will prioritise targets closest to it, regardless whether its a tank or infantry, thats fine but what if you have tanks shooting at your tank, but your tank decides to target infantry instead because its closer, thats a problem. 

Another issue is tank destroyers randomly rotating 360 for no apparent reasons or positioning themselves sideways and refusing to return to their original position, turrets on tanks remain in their last position instead of facing forward which makes it very easy for enemies to destroy your tanks. 

Infantry cannot even reliably use smoke nor AT weapons to target vehicles within range, trying to give commands to infantry only registers half the time, infantry will often run up to a tank and try to throw an AT grenade and then get gunned down before they are able to, infantry are also completely inept at moving around on their own, get into cover or throw smoke automatically, this game makes it all a manual process which is ridicules. 

Even Korean RTS masters would struggle to control so many units all at the same time manually, it should not be necessary. 

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
Because the AI is so broken, this game is best suited for short game sessions of 15 to 30 minutes in its two multiplayer modes, Domination or Battle Zones which is basically Capture Points. 

The singleplayer is all over the place, some missions are well made, most are not however, extremely tedious smoke spamming and using snipers and field guns to plow your way through, because like I said the AI is extremely basic in this game, with that also comes with features like no suppression mechanic, no aiming delay, troops in this game have instant reaction time, 100% accuracy within 100 metres which by itself is ridicules and they all share a global vision system, no field of view for individual troops meaning artillery at the end of the map can somehow communicate with infantry dude at the other end which even CoH2 stopped doing. 
And if you play on higher difficulties, the enemy AI gets more health AND tanks also gets more ARMOUR! And they do more damage against you, this is essentially just cheat mode for AI. 

There is also a conquest mode which lets you fight AI on a quasi combat theatre where you attack, then defend, the maps you get to fight on are usually randomised, here you attack certain points on the theatre to gain resources or manpower etc this sounds brilliant but the AI basically just stays still on attack mode and they wont even chase you, on defensive mode, they throw everything they have at you in what can only be described as a zombie wave, there no strategy involved, its just pure unit spam, this gets real old after the 50th time.  

At least in multiplayer PvE, the AI will indeed defend and attack in one battle which makes it a bit more engaging gameplay wise. 

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
[list]
    [*]Amazing sounds, good art direction makes this aesthetically pleasing to look at.
    [*]AI is extremely basic, cheats a lot in higher difficulties makes it frustrating to play against.
    [*]Way too many weird AI behaviours makes long game sessions frustrating and not fun. 
    [*]Most game modes are not fun to play, takes way too long and frustrating because of the poor AI design.
    [*]Tedious micro management of everything, to avoid tank destroyers from rotating all the time, you have to turn off the engine, stupid way of dealing with game yank.
    [*]Developers have promised AI improvement for multiple years, but spends more time making degrading community posts about how people should stop whining. 
    [*]Multiplayer PvP is difficult to play because of cheese and extremely bad network code which is tied to Steam Workshop servers, so if Steam goes down, GoH goes down. Almost all players are either from China or Russia, meaning you will constantly face players with 200+ ping.
[/list]

Do I recommend this game? No, if you can get it on sale, thats different story, but for a full price there better ways to spend your time.
I do love the game concept, but as a video game its hard pill to swallow, the only fun I have in GoH is to play with friends, in short sessions that usually lasts maximum of 40 minutes, and we play maybe one or two a few days a week at most against AI on veterancy, in hardcore difficulty, the AI’s mortars for some reasons have 90% hit ratio, which may not sound too bad but remember in veterancy its only 30% meaning almost every shot will hit your infantry directly, I had one enemy mortar destroy my Tiger 1 because yes of course the mortar shell is now also more POWERFUL! If I wanted to play against cheaters this much, I just boot up BF1 or Hunt Showdown.

Game is quite fun when it works properly. Let down by the absolute braindead decisions of your troop AI. Why try and shoot at the tank which is 20 meters away blasting the AT gun you're currently manning when there's another one half way across the map doing nothing. 

Could be excused if the AI would actually listen to you when you tell them to attack something, but often they straight up don't follow your commands (e.g. the AT gun, told it to attack the tank in front of it - they swing it to face but then don't even shoot and instantly rotate it back to shoot at the other tank, no surprises the close tank blows them and the gun to pieces). 

Soldiers often won't shoot someone right in front of them, or get stuck in animations. They also tend to run out of ammo quite quickly, you then have to micromanage them to run back to a truck or crate or dead comrade to rearm with some rather unintuitive controls. Doesn't need a lot of modding to be good. Campaign and multiplayer modes as envisioned by the developer are not terribly good-so why recommend this? Because despite poor demonstrations by the developer-this game is rich with tools and mechanisms for one to make World War 2 battles at all kinds of scales. Don't buy this game for the stock campaigns and modes, buy it for the development tools. Learning to make use of the GEM Editor is a tough but extremely rewarding task. One can make everything from the Brecourt Manor assault to the Battle of Kursk convincingly in this game, and it's incredible that the engine can manage to do both kinds of battle. This game might be one of the only ways to do the varied kinds of fighting that took place in the Second World War any real justice. 

If that's not in your interest, there is still a robust (if over simplistic) campaign generator and multiplayer scene to make this game worth the purchase with its most basic tools. There is a large and vibrant modding community supporting this game as much as the developer is however and they're creating all kinds of content for the game from enhanced weather to Star Wars. There are plenty of World War 2 action games-but this is the only one that can fit absolutely all of them inside of it, if you're willing to learn a bit...

Tl:dr buy this game for the development tools, not the shipped content. Learn a little and it will  yield a lot.

I'm pretty sure there are more issues, and the ones I mentioned are the glaring ones.

In conclusion, "Gates of Hell" comes highly recommended, especially when augmented with mods like the Valour Mod. + Terrain matters. Using real military tactics such as combined arms , flanking, overlapping fields of fire, placing units in defilade and enfilading the enemy are essential. As in real life, such tactics will win you the engagement while minimising casualties. Scouting and reconnaissance, in particular, are vital. You need to see the enemy before he finds you. Blindly charging a tank over a hill into entrenched enemy positions' fields of fire is not a winning tactic. 
+ In addition to the top-down RTS point of view, the game adds a fun (but slightly clunky) first-person mode allowing control of individual units. 
+ The base game includes three major modes of play: a set of single-player missions, a dynamic conquest mode, and finally, multiplayer. 
+ The single player campaign mode comprises lovingly-crafted scripted missions based on historic engagements on the Eastern and Finnish fronts. Each can take hours to play. They range from infantry squad-level to almost company-level engagements. There are 10 German, 10 Russian and six Finnish missions if you have both DLCs. The single player mode now also include skirmish battles, which are a little like PVP against the AI on big maps for control points, which confer new unit types.
+ Conquest mode sees you fighting a series of offensive and defensive battles across a rudimentary but dynamic campaign map, unlocking better and better units with research points that you earn by winning. Good replay value here. 
+ Multiplayer mode, with a couple of options, domination and conquest. You can also play with and against the AI on a variety of settings. Multiplayer is satisfying, requiring you to trade off holding key points while spending population and doctrine  points to bring in new units. Fast micro wins the day. 
+ The terrain is destructible. You can lay mine fields, dig emplacements, call in artillery and aircraft strafing runs or watch rocket weapons level enemy positions in enormous explosions that wreck buildings and rock the screen.
+ Weapon engagement distances are much longer than comparable games. They aren't completely realistic, but artillery and tank cannons can reach far further than you might be used to in other games. This is great, because as in real life, deploying your forces thoughtfully and with good lines of sight is essential. That said, it is not even close to the reality of the time by an order of magnitude. For example, the Wehrmacht's famed 7.5cm Pak 40's engagement range was 1,800 metres. In the game it is modelled at around one-tenth of this. 
+ A range of difficulty, economy and other levels helps you tweak the game into an experience that suits you. 
+ Includes a vast range of historically accurate German, Russian (and with the DLC) Finnish units ranging from infantry, armoured fighting vehicles of all types, anti-aircraft and artillery weapons, aircraft (as call-ins) and so on. 
+ Even individual infantrymen have names, unique features and inventories. Your units can repair and man broken equipment, swap and replenish items in their inventories, pick up discarded weapons, and so on. Supply is modelled too: units need ammunition, and fuel if a vehicle, which must be replenished. 
+ Lively mod community making everything from punishing campaigns to helpful tweaks. 
+ Good sound, music and increasingly great graphics even on the more modest rigs.
+ The developers do a great job of staying in touch with the community, delivering content above and beyond, and, above all, regularly patching bugs. 

But: 

- Steep learning curve. There's almost zero help documentation and only one clunky tutorial mission. On-screen information is often hard to understand acronyms, e.g. the PVP points. Not many user guides or YouTube Let's Play videos. Means it takes determination and time to get the meta. Suggest trying an easier AI with the Fog of War off to get the hang of it. 
- Micro-intensive. Can easily become overwhelming. Battles turn against you swiftly if you don't pay attention and lose a key unit. It's essential to plan and execute rapidly so you have to learn keyboard shortcuts and have good micro.
- Unit pathfinding is bad. If units sniff the slightest opportunity to snarl themselves up on a road or get tangled in a tree, they will. Drive vehicles yourself if in any doubt. 
- The single player campaigns are not linked by a story and characters, if that matters to you.
- The conquest and multiplayer AI opponents aren't smart. They tend to throw units at you piecemeal in predictable waves with few attempts to flank you or use terrain to advantage.
- Not easy to find multiplayer opponents depending on where you are in the world. 
- Does not model morale, fatigue and other human characteristics in the way, say, Total War does. Units don't run away, for instance. 
- No cinematic replay feature so you can watch at your leisure and screen grab a battle after you have won it. 
- Some models still look a bit 1990s, such as soldiers' arms. 

It's the most realistic WW2 RTS on the market but maybe not suited to a casual gamer. I recommend it if you want a well-supported but demanding, semi-realistic WW2 RTS and are prepared to put the time in.
